learn.hook: How much rain fell over a day if you know the rate every hour? Add up rate × time: that is a definite integral, and one theorem makes it easy.
points: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the area under y = f(x) between x = a and x = b, above the x-axis, when f ≥ 0. a and b are the lower and upper limits.
Area function: A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt.
First fundamental theorem: A′(x) = f(x) for continuous f.
Second fundamental theorem: if F′ = f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). The constant C cancels, so ignore it.
Definite integral as the limit of a sum is not in the current CBSE syllabus.

example.q: Evaluate ∫₁² x³ dx.

learn.reallife: If a rain gauge records the rainfall rate (mm per hour) through the day, the total rainfall for the day is the definite integral of that rate over time.

games.title: Fundamental theorem facts
items: By the first fundamental theorem, A′(x) = f(x).
We must add + C in a definite integral.
It is F(b) − F(a): upper limit minus lower limit.

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀² (x² + 1) dx.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to integrate the constant 1

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) cos x dx.
quiz.mistake: Uses −sin x as the anti-derivative

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x²).
quiz.explain: [tan⁻¹x]₀¹ = π/4 − 0.
quiz.mistake: Confuses tan⁻¹ with log

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₁^e log x dx.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that log 1 = 0 and log e = 1

quiz.q: If F(x) = ∫₀ˣ cos t dt, what is F′(π/3)?
quiz.explain: By the first fundamental theorem, F′(x) = cos x, so F′(π/3) = cos(π/3) = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Integrates cos t again instead of using A′(x) = f(x)

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₂³ dx/(x² − 1).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 1/(2a) factor

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2.
Reason (R): The anti-derivative of sin x is −cos x, so the integral is −cos π + cos 0.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: −cos π + cos 0 = 1 + 1 = 2. R is the fundamental-theorem calculation behind A.
steps: R: ∫sin x dx = −cos x, so the integral is −cos π − (−cos 0) — true
−cos π + cos 0 = 1 + 1 = 2, so A is true
A is calculated exactly as R says
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Uses +cos x as the anti-derivative and gets 0

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I evaluate ∫ from a to b without adding up tiny strips?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Find any anti-derivative F, then F(b) − F(a). The fundamental theorem does the strip-adding for you!
teach.nudge: Which limit goes first in the subtraction?

revise.summary: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) where F is any anti-derivative, so C cancels. The area function A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt has A′(x) = f(x).
focus: Evaluate definite integrals with the second fundamental theorem
Differentiate an area function
Use standard anti-derivatives at the limits
traps: Subtract in the order F(b) − F(a)
Don't use +cos x as the anti-derivative of sin x
Don't integrate again when F′(x) is asked

learn.hook: When you substitute in a definite integral, change the limits too. Then you never have to switch back to x.
points: Put t = g(x), dt = g′(x) dx, and change the limits: x = a gives t = g(a), x = b gives t = g(b).
Then ∫ₐᵇ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx = ∫ from g(a) to g(b) of f(t) dt.
Do not mix: either change limits and stay in t, or go back to x and use the old limits.
∫₀¹ 2x/(1 + x²) dx = log 2 (t = 1 + x², t from 1 to 2).
∫₀¹ tan⁻¹x/(1 + x²) dx = π²/32 (t = tan⁻¹x, t from 0 to π/4).

example.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin x cos x dx.
steps: Put t = sin x, dt = cos x dx.

learn.reallife: Railway engineers converting a curved track's length integral into a simpler one change the variable and limits together, exactly as here.

games.title: Evaluate ∫₀¹ 2x(x² + 1)³ dx
items: Put t = x² + 1, so dt = 2x dx
Change limits: x = 0 → t = 1, x = 1 → t = 2

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x/(x² + 1) dx.
quiz.explain: t = x² + 1, dt = 2x dx, limits 1 to 2: (1/2)∫₁² dt/t = (1/2) log 2.
steps: Put t = x² + 1, dt = 2x dx; x = 0 → t = 1, x = 1 → t = 2
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 1/2 from dt = 2x dx

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ tan⁻¹x/(1 + x²) dx.
quiz.explain: t = tan⁻¹x, t from 0 to π/4: ∫t dt = (π/4)²/2 = π²/32.
steps: Put t = tan⁻¹x, dt = dx/(1 + x²); limits 0 → 0, 1 → π/4
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve when integrating t

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ sin⁻¹x/√(1 − x²) dx.
quiz.explain: t = sin⁻¹x, t from 0 to π/2: [t²/2] = π²/8.
steps: Put t = sin⁻¹x, dt = dx/√(1 − x²); limits 0 → 0, 1 → π/2
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change the limits

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx.
quiz.explain: t = x², dt = 2x dx: (1/2)∫₀¹ eᵗ dt = (e − 1)/2.
steps: Put t = x², dt = 2x dx; limits 0 → 0, 1 → 1
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 1/2

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₁^e (log x)/x dx.
quiz.explain: t = log x, from 0 to 1: ∫₀¹ t dt = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the old limits 1 and e after substituting

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) cos x/(1 + sin x) dx.
quiz.explain: t = 1 + sin x, from 1 to 2: ∫dt/t = log 2.
steps: Put t = 1 + sin x, dt = cos x dx; x = 0 → t = 1, x = π/2 → t = 2
quiz.mistake: Loses track of the limits

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin x) cos⁵x dx using t = sin x. The resulting t-integral is
quiz.explain: cos⁵x dx = cos⁴x · cos x dx = (1 − t²)² dt, and limits become 0 to 1.
steps: Put t = sin x, dt = cos x dx; x = 0 → 0, x = π/2 → 1
cos⁵x dx = cos⁴x · cos x dx = (1 − sin²x)² cos x dx = (1 − t²)² dt
quiz.mistake: Keeps the x-limits after substitution

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): After substituting t = g(x) in ∫ₐᵇ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx, we may evaluate the t-integral using the new limits g(a) and g(b), without returning to x.
Reason (R): As x runs from a to b, t = g(x) runs from g(a) to g(b), and f(g(x)) g′(x) dx becomes f(t) dt.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: R is exactly the substitution rule for definite integrals: the integrand turns into f(t) dt and the limits turn into g(a) and g(b). So A is true and R is its reason.
steps: R: as x goes a → b, t = g(x) goes g(a) → g(b), and f(g(x)) g′(x) dx = f(t) dt — true
So the t-integral with limits g(a), g(b) equals the original: A is true
R is the justification for A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the old x-limits must be used after substituting

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'When I substitute in a definite integral, what happens to the limits?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Change the limits along with the variable, then finish in t. No need to go back to x!
teach.nudge: If x runs from 0 to 1 and t = x² + 1, where does t run?

revise.summary: In a definite integral, substitute t = g(x) and change the limits to g(a) and g(b); then finish in t without returning to x.
focus: Choose t and find dt
Convert both limits correctly
Evaluate the t-integral
remember: ∫ₐᵇ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx = ∫ from g(a) to g(b) of f(t) dt
traps: Don't keep the old x-limits after substituting
Don't forget factors like 1/2 from dt = 2x dx
Don't mix x-limits with a t-integral

topics.title: Properties of definite integrals I and modulus integrals

learn.hook: Some definite integrals that look impossible fall in two lines, not by integrating harder but by using a property cleverly.
points: P0: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(t) dt (the variable is a dummy).
P1: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = −∫ from b to a of f(x) dx; in particular ∫ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0.
P2: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᶜ f(x) dx + ∫ from c to b of f(x) dx for any c.
P3: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx. Adding the two versions often cancels the hard part.
Modulus: split at the zeros of the expression inside |…| and integrate each piece with the correct sign.

example.q: Evaluate ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of dx/(1 + √(tan x)).
steps: Write tan x = sin x/cos x: I = ∫√cos x/(√cos x + √sin x) dx.
P3 (a + b = π/2) turns cos ↔ sin: I = ∫√sin x/(√sin x + √cos x) dx.
Add: 2I = ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of 1 dx = π/6.

learn.reallife: A scooter goes forward and then comes back. To find the total distance (not the net displacement), you split the velocity integral where the velocity changes sign, just like a modulus integral.

games.title: Evaluate ∫₀⁴ |x − 1| dx
items: x − 1 = 0 at x = 1, so split at 1

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₋₁² |x³ − x| dx.
quiz.explain: Sign of x³ − x: + on [−1, 0], − on [0, 1], + on [1, 2]. The pieces are 1/4, 1/4 and 9/4, total 11/4.
quiz.mistake: Integrates x³ − x without splitting and gets 9/4

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀⁴ |x − 1| dx.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the modulus and gets 4

quiz.q: If ∫₀³ f(x) dx = 7 and ∫₀¹ f(x) dx = 2, what is ∫₁³ f(x) dx?
quiz.explain: By P2, ∫₀³ = ∫₀¹ + ∫₁³, so ∫₁³ f = 7 − 2 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Adds the integrals instead of subtracting

quiz.q: If ∫₁⁴ f(x) dx = 6, what is ∫₄¹ f(x) dx?
quiz.explain: Reversing the limits changes the sign (P1).
quiz.mistake: Thinks the order of limits does not matter

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of dx/(1 + √(tan x)).
quiz.explain: Using P3 and adding the two forms, 2I = π/3 − π/6 = π/6, so I = π/12.
steps: I = ∫√cos x/(√cos x + √sin x) dx; P3 with a + b = π/2 swaps sin ↔ cos
I = ∫√sin x/(√sin x + √cos x) dx; add: 2I = ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of 1 dx
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve after adding the two integrals

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₂⁸ |x − 5| dx.
quiz.explain: Split at 5: ∫₂⁵ (5 − x) dx = 9/2 and ∫₅⁸ (x − 5) dx = 9/2. Total 9.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the modulus and gets 0 or a wrong value

quiz.q: Applying P3 to ∫₀² x(2 − x) dx gives which integral?
quiz.explain: P3 replaces x by 0 + 2 − x = 2 − x, turning x(2 − x) into (2 − x)x, the same function.
steps: P3 on [0, 2]: replace x by 0 + 2 − x = 2 − x
Answer: ∫₀² (2 − x)x dx, the same integral
quiz.mistake: Thinks P3 always changes the integrand

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0 for any integrable f.
Reason (R): ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = −∫ from b to a of f(x) dx.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Put b = a in R: I = −I, so I = 0. R gives A directly.
steps: Put b = a: I = −I ⇒ 2I = 0 ⇒ I = 0, so A is true from R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal limits give f(a)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I integrate |x − 1| from 0 to 4?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Split where the inside is zero, use the right sign on each piece, and add. Modulus tamed!
teach.nudge: Where do you split the interval?

revise.summary: Definite integrals can be split at any point, change sign when the limits are swapped, and satisfy ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx. Modulus integrals are split at the zeros inside the modulus.
focus: Evaluate modulus integrals by splitting
Use P2 to find a missing piece
Use P3 and add to cancel the hard part
remember: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx
traps: Don't integrate |f| without splitting at its zeros
Halve after adding I to itself
Swapping limits changes the sign

topics.title: Properties II: even, odd and classic results

learn.hook: ∫ from −1 to 1 of sin⁵x cos⁴x dx: no integration needed. The answer is 0, and symmetry tells you why.
points: P4: ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx.
P5: ∫₀^(2a) f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx if f(2a − x) = f(x), and = 0 if f(2a − x) = −f(x).
P6: ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx if f is even (f(−x) = f(x)), and = 0 if f is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)).
Classic: ∫₀^(π/2) sinⁿx/(sinⁿx + cosⁿx) dx = π/4 for every n; ∫₀^(π/2) log sin x dx = −(π/2) log 2.
Strategy for any integral: simplify, try substitution, partial fractions, parts, then properties.

example.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin x)/(√(sin x) + √(cos x)) dx.
steps: Call it I. By P4, replacing x with π/2 − x: I = ∫₀^(π/2) √(cos x)/(√(cos x) + √(sin x)) dx.

learn.reallife: Physicists use symmetry all the time: an odd function integrates to zero over symmetric limits, so whole parts of a long calculation cancel instantly.

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₋₁¹ sin⁵x cos⁴x dx.
quiz.explain: f(−x) = (−sin x)⁵ cos⁴x = −f(x), so f is odd and the integral over [−1, 1] is 0.
steps: f(x) = sin⁵x cos⁴x; f(−x) = (−sin x)⁵(cos x)⁴ = −f(x): odd
P6: integral of an odd function over [−a, a] is 0
quiz.mistake: Tries to integrate directly instead of using odd symmetry

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₋₂² x² dx.
quiz.explain: x² is even: 2∫₀² x² dx = 2 × 8/3 = 16/3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every integral over symmetric limits is 0

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x(1 − x)⁵ dx.
quiz.explain: By P4, it equals ∫₀¹ (1 − x)x⁵ dx = 1/6 − 1/7 = 1/42.
quiz.mistake: Expands (1 − x)⁵ and makes an arithmetic slip

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁴x/(sin⁴x + cos⁴x) dx.
quiz.explain: Adding I with its P4 version gives 2I = π/2, so I = π/4, whatever the power.
steps: I = ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁴x/(sin⁴x + cos⁴x) dx; P4 (x → π/2 − x) gives I = ∫cos⁴x/(cos⁴x + sin⁴x) dx
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(2π) cos⁵x dx.
quiz.explain: cos(2π − x) = cos x gives 2∫₀^π cos⁵x dx, and cos(π − x) = −cos x makes ∫₀^π cos⁵x dx = 0.
steps: P5 with 2a = 2π: cos(2π − x) = cos x, so I = 2∫₀^π cos⁵x dx
P5 with 2a = π: cos⁵(π − x) = −cos⁵x, so ∫₀^π cos⁵x dx = 0
quiz.mistake: Applies only the first half of P5

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) log sin x dx.
quiz.explain: Adding I with ∫ log cos x and using sin x cos x = (sin 2x)/2 gives 2I = I − (π/2) log 2, so I = −(π/2) log 2.
steps: I = ∫₀^(π/2) log sin x dx = ∫₀^(π/2) log cos x dx (by P4)
2I = ∫ log(sin x cos x) dx = ∫ log sin 2x dx − (π/2) log 2
Put t = 2x: ∫₀^(π/2) log sin 2x dx = (1/2)∫₀^π log sin t dt = I
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign wrong; log sin x ≤ 0 on (0, π/2)

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^π x sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx.
quiz.explain: P4 gives I = π∫₀^π sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx − I, so 2I = π[−tan⁻¹(cos x)]₀^π = π(π/2), and I = π²/4.
steps: P4: I = ∫₀^π (π − x) sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx
Add: 2I = π∫₀^π sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx = π[−tan⁻¹(cos x)]₀^π
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve after moving I across

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫₋π/2^π/2 sin⁷x dx = 0.
Reason (R): sin⁷x is an odd function.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: sin⁷(−x) = −sin⁷x, so by P6 the integral over a symmetric interval is 0.
steps: R: sin⁷(−x) = (−sin x)⁷ = −sin⁷x, so sin⁷x is odd — true
P6: an odd function over [−π/2, π/2] integrates to 0, so A is true
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks odd powers of sin are even functions

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How can an integral be zero without integrating at all?'
teach.praise: Tweet! An odd function over −a to a has equal and opposite areas that cancel to zero. Symmetry is a superpower!
teach.nudge: What kind of function gives zero, and over what kind of limits?

revise.summary: ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx; over [−a, a], even functions give twice the half-integral and odd functions give 0. Classic results include π/4 for sinⁿ/(sinⁿ + cosⁿ) and −(π/2) log 2.
focus: Use odd/even symmetry
Apply P4 and add the two forms
Use P5 for intervals like [0, 2π]
traps: Not every integral over symmetric limits is 0; only odd functions
Don't forget to halve after adding
log sin x ≤ 0 on (0, π/2), so its integral is negative

topics.title: Area under a curve: vertical and horizontal strips

learn.hook: Slice a region into thin strips, add their areas, and shrink the strips to zero width. That sum becomes a definite integral.
points: Definite integrals give areas of regions bounded by curves, lines and the axes.
Vertical strips: the area between y = f(x) ≥ 0, the x-axis and the lines x = a, x = b is ∫ₐᵇ y dx.
Horizontal strips: the area between x = g(y) ≥ 0, the y-axis and y = c, y = d is ∫ from c to d of x dy.
A straight line region is a trapezium or triangle, so you can check the integral with geometry.
Always sketch first: it tells you which strips to use and where the limits are.

example.q: Find the area bounded by y = x², the x-axis and the lines x = 1 and x = 2.
steps: The curve lies above the x-axis on [1, 2].

learn.reallife: Surveyors estimate the area of a plot with a curved boundary by measuring its width at regular intervals and adding thin strips, which is integration in practice.

games.title: Find an area by integration
items: Sketch the curve and the bounding lines
Write the area as ∫ y dx or ∫ x dy with limits
Write the answer in square units

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by y = x³, the x-axis and the lines x = 1 and x = 2 (square units).
quiz.explain: Area = ∫₁² x³ dx = [x⁴/4]₁² = 4 − 1/4 = 15/4.
quiz.mistake: Integrates x² by mistake

quiz.q: Find the area under y = 2x + 1 from x = 0 to x = 2 (square units).
quiz.explain: ∫₀² (2x + 1) dx = [x² + x]₀² = 6. As a trapezium: (1/2)(1 + 5)(2) = 6.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the constant term

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by x = y², the y-axis and the lines y = 1 and y = 3 (square units).
quiz.explain: Using horizontal strips, area = ∫₁³ y² dy = [y³/3]₁³ = 9 − 1/3 = 26/3.
quiz.mistake: Uses vertical strips with the wrong limits

quiz.q: For the area between a curve x = g(y), the y-axis and y = c to y = d, which integral is used?
options: ∫ from c to d of y dx
∫ from c to d of y dy
∫ from c to d of x dx
∫ from c to d of x dy
quiz.explain: Horizontal strips have length x and width dy.
steps: Horizontal strips: length = x = g(y), thickness = dy
Add the strips from y = c to y = d
Answer: ∫ from c to d of x dy
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which variable is the strip width

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by y = √x, the x-axis and x = 9 (square units).
quiz.mistake: Uses 3/2 instead of 2/3

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by y = eˣ, the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 1.
quiz.explain: ∫₀¹ eˣ dx = e − 1.
steps: eˣ > 0, so the region is above the x-axis
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract e⁰ = 1

quiz.q: The area under y = 4 − x² between x = 0 and x = 2 (above the x-axis) is
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The area of the triangle bounded by y = x, the x-axis and x = 4 is 8 square units.
Reason (R): Area = ∫₀⁴ x dx = 8.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
steps: y = x ≥ 0 on [0, 4], so the integral is the area: A is true
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks integration and geometry give different answers

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does an integral give me the area under a curve?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Thin strips of height y and width dx, added from a to b. That is ∫ y dx. Area unlocked!
teach.nudge: What does each strip look like, and how are the strips combined?

revise.summary: The area between y = f(x) ≥ 0, the x-axis and x = a, x = b is ∫ₐᵇ y dx; with horizontal strips, the area next to the y-axis is ∫ x dy. Sketch first to pick strips and limits.
focus: Find areas under curves like x², x³, √x, eˣ
Use horizontal strips for curves x = g(y)
Check line regions with geometry
remember: Horizontal strips: Area = ∫ from c to d of x dy
traps: Don't mix up dx and dy strips
Subtract the lower-limit value, e.g. e⁰ = 1
Use the right power: ∫√x dx = (2/3)x^(3/2)

topics.title: Regions below the axis and on both sides

learn.hook: ∫₀^(2π) sin x dx = 0, yet the curve clearly encloses area with the axis. Integrals can cancel; areas never do.
points: If f(x) ≤ 0 on [a, b], the region lies below the x-axis and its area is |∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx|.
If the curve crosses the axis at c, split: Area = |∫ₐᶜ f dx| + |∫ from c to b of f dx|.
y = sin x on [0, 2π] gives area 2 + 2 = 4, though the integral is 0. Similarly y = cos x on [0, 2π] gives area 4.
y = x³ on [−2, 1] gives area 4 + 1/4 = 17/4.
Modulus curves like y = |x + 3| lie above the axis: integrate piece by piece.

example.q: Find the area bounded by y = cos x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2π.
steps: Pieces: ∫₀^(π/2) cos x = 1, |∫ from π/2 to 3π/2 of cos x| = 2, ∫ from 3π/2 to 2π of cos x = 1.

learn.reallife: A bank account's net change over a month can be zero even when lots of money went in and out. The total money moved adds the absolute amounts, just as area adds the pieces above and below the axis as positives.

games.title: Area or integral?
items: The positive and negative parts cancel.
The area between y = sin x and the x-axis on [0, 2π] is 0.
For f ≤ 0 on [a, b], the area is −∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx.
The integral is negative, so its negative is the area.
Area must always be split where the curve crosses the axis.
Otherwise positive and negative parts cancel.
The area between y = x³ and the x-axis on [−1, 1] is 0.

items.q: Area: y = sin x, x = 0 to π
Area: y = sin x, x = 0 to 2π

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by y = sin x and the x-axis between x = 0 and x = 2π.
quiz.explain: ∫₀^π sin x = 2 and |∫ from π to 2π of sin x| = 2. Total area = 4.
quiz.mistake: Reports the integral 0 instead of the area

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by y = x³, the x-axis and the lines x = −2 and x = 1.
quiz.explain: |∫₋₂⁰ x³ dx| = 4 and ∫₀¹ x³ dx = 1/4, total 17/4.
quiz.mistake: Integrates straight across and gets −15/4

quiz.q: Find the area between y = 3x + 2, the x-axis and the lines x = −1 and x = 1.
quiz.explain: The line crosses at x = −2/3. Below: 1/6. Above: 25/6. Total 26/6 = 13/3.
quiz.mistake: Integrates without splitting and gets 4

quiz.q: Find the area under y = |x + 3| from x = −6 to x = 0.
quiz.explain: Two triangles each with base 3 and height 3: 9/2 + 9/2 = 9.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one triangle

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by y = x² − 1 and the x-axis between x = −1 and x = 1.
quiz.explain: The curve is below the axis there: ∫₋₁¹ (x² − 1) dx = 2/3 − 2 = −4/3, so the area is 4/3.
quiz.mistake: Reports the negative integral as the area

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by y = cos x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = π.
quiz.explain: 1 from [0, π/2] plus |−1| from [π/2, π] = 2.
quiz.mistake: Integrates straight across and gets 0

quiz.q: Why can ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx be smaller than the area between the curve and the x-axis?
options: Because area is measured in square units
Parts below the axis give negative contributions that cancel positive parts
quiz.explain: Integrals are signed; area counts every part as positive.
steps: A definite integral is signed: parts below the axis count as negative
Area counts every part as positive
So negative parts cancel some positive parts in the integral
Answer: Parts below the axis give negative contributions that cancel positive parts
quiz.mistake: Treats the integral as always equal to the area

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The area bounded by y = x, the x-axis, x = −2 and x = 2 is 4 square units.
Reason (R): ∫₋₂² x dx = 0.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Area = 2 + 2 = 4 (two triangles). R is true too, but it is the signed integral, which is exactly why it cannot explain the area.
steps: Area: triangle on [−2, 0] (area 2) + triangle on [0, 2] (area 2) = 4, so A is true
The zero integral does not give the area 4, so R does not explain A
Answer: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
quiz.mistake: Thinks a zero integral means zero area

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: 'The integral of sin x from 0 to 2π is 0. So is the area 0 too?'
teach.praise: Chirp! No! Split where the curve crosses the axis and add absolute values. Area is 4, not 0!
teach.nudge: What do you do with the part of the curve below the x-axis?

revise.summary: Parts of a region below the x-axis give negative integrals, so take absolute values and split the region where the curve crosses the axis. The area can be positive even when the integral is 0.
focus: Split at the points where the curve crosses the x-axis
Find areas for sin x, cos x, x³ and lines on both sides
Handle modulus curves piece by piece
remember: Area below the axis = |∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx|
y = sin x on [0, 2π]: area 4, integral 0
traps: Don't report a negative or zero integral as the area
Don't integrate across a crossing point without splitting
Area is always positive

topics.title: Area of a circle and an ellipse

learn.hook: You have used πr² since Class 7. Now prove it with calculus, and get the ellipse's area πab for free.
points: Circle x² + y² = a²: by symmetry, area = 4 × (first-quadrant area) = 4∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx.
Using ∫√(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a), the first quadrant gives (a²/2)(π/2) = πa²/4, so the area is πa².
Ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1: y = (b/a)√(a² − x²) in the first quadrant, so area = 4(b/a)∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx = πab.
A circle is the ellipse with a = b.
Use symmetry about both axes to integrate over one quadrant only.

example.q: Find the area enclosed by the ellipse x²/16 + y²/9 = 1.

learn.reallife: Planetary orbits are ellipses. ISRO's Mangalyaan orbit around Mars was elliptical, and Kepler's second law links area swept by an orbit to time, so these area formulas matter in mission planning.

games.title: Area of the circle x² + y² = a²
items: First quadrant: y = √(a² − x²), x from 0 to a

quiz.q: Find the area enclosed by the circle x² + y² = 9.
quiz.explain: Area = πa² with a = 3, i.e. 9π.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2πa (the circumference) or a⁴

quiz.q: Find the area of the region in the first quadrant enclosed by x² + y² = 16 and the axes.
quiz.explain: One quarter of π(4²) = 16π/4 = 4π.
quiz.mistake: Gives the full circle's area

quiz.q: Find the area enclosed by x²/4 + y²/9 = 1.
quiz.explain: a = 2, b = 3, area = πab = 6π.
quiz.mistake: Uses a² and b² instead of a and b

quiz.q: In finding the area of the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, the first-quadrant integral is
quiz.explain: Solving for y gives y = (b/a)√(a² − x²) with x from 0 to a.
steps: Solve for y: y² = b²(1 − x²/a²) ⇒ y = (b/a)√(a² − x²) (first quadrant)
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio when solving for y

quiz.q: What is ∫₀³ √(9 − x²) dx?
quiz.explain: It is a quarter of the area of a circle of radius 3: 9π/4.
steps: y = √(9 − x²), 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 is a quarter of the circle of radius 3
quiz.mistake: Takes a half instead of a quarter of the circle

quiz.q: Find the area enclosed by 4x² + 9y² = 36.
quiz.explain: Divide by 36: x²/9 + y²/4 = 1, so a = 3, b = 2 and area = 6π.
quiz.mistake: Uses the coefficients 4 and 9 as a and b

quiz.q: For the circle x² + y² = a², which value of ∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx is correct?
quiz.explain: (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) from 0 to a = (a²/2)(π/2) = πa²/4.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to evaluate sin⁻¹(1) = π/2

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The area enclosed by x² + y² = a² is πa².
Reason (R): The area enclosed by x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 is πab.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A circle is the special ellipse with b = a, so R gives π · a · a = πa².
steps: A circle x² + y² = a² is the ellipse with b = a
π · a · a = πa², so A follows from R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not see the circle as a special ellipse

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can calculus prove that the area of a circle is πr²?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Integrate √(a² − x²) over one quarter, get πa²/4, and multiply by 4. πr² proved!
teach.nudge: Why do we only integrate over one quadrant?

revise.summary: Using symmetry and the formula for ∫√(a² − x²) dx, the circle x² + y² = a² has area πa² and the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 has area πab.
focus: Find areas of circles and ellipses (whole or a quarter)
Rewrite equations like 4x² + 9y² = 36 in standard form
Set up the first-quadrant integral
traps: Use a and b, not a² and b²
Divide to get 1 on the right side before reading a and b
Don't confuse area πa² with circumference 2πa

learn.hook: A satellite dish has a parabolic cross-section. How much area does the parabola enclose up to a given line? Two neat formulas answer it.
points: For y² = 4ax and x = k: the region is symmetric about the x-axis, so area = 2∫₀ᵏ 2√(ax) dx = (8/3)√a · k^(3/2).
For x² = 4ay and y = k: area = 2∫₀ᵏ 2√(ay) dy.
First-quadrant regions: use only y ≥ 0, x ≥ 0 and the given lines as limits.
Choose strips wisely: for x² = 4y and the y-axis, horizontal strips (∫ x dy) are often easier.
Area between two curves and between a curve and a slanting line are not in the current CBSE syllabus.

example.q: Find the area bounded by y² = 9x, x = 2, x = 4 and the x-axis in the first quadrant.

learn.reallife: Parabolic solar cookers concentrate sunlight at the focus; the cross-section of the reflector is a parabola, and its area is found with integrals like these.

items.q: y = x², y-axis, y = 1 to y = 4 (first quadrant)

games.title: Parabola region facts
items: y² = 4ax is symmetric about the x-axis.
Replacing y by −y leaves it unchanged.
For x² = 4y and y = k, the area is 2∫₀ᵏ 2√y dy.
x = ±2√y, so each half has width 2√y.
The area between y² = 4x and x = 1 is ∫₀¹ 2√x dx.
That is only the upper half; the full area is twice this.
Area between two curves is in the current CBSE syllabus.
It has been removed in the rationalised book.
In the first quadrant, y² = 9x gives y = 3√x.

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by y² = 4x and the line x = 1.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the upper half

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by x² = 4y and the line y = 4.
quiz.explain: Area = ∫₀⁴ 2x dy with x = 2√y: ∫₀⁴ 4√y dy = (8/3)(8) = 64/3.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one side of the y-axis

quiz.q: Find the area of the first-quadrant region bounded by y = x², the y-axis and the line y = 4.
quiz.explain: Horizontal strips: ∫₀⁴ √y dy = (2/3)(8) = 16/3.
quiz.mistake: Uses vertical strips with x from 0 to 4

quiz.q: Find the area bounded by y² = 9x, x = 2, x = 4 and the x-axis in the first quadrant.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 3 from y = 3√x

quiz.q: Find the area of the first-quadrant region bounded by x² = 4y, the y-axis, y = 2 and y = 4.
steps: First quadrant: x = 2√y; horizontal strips from y = 2 to y = 4
quiz.mistake: Uses 4√y, which counts both sides of the y-axis

quiz.q: For the parabola y² = 4ax and the line x = a, the enclosed area is
steps: Symmetric about the x-axis: area = 2∫₀ᵃ 2√(ax) dx
quiz.mistake: Counts only one half

quiz.q: Find the area of the first-quadrant region bounded by y = x², the y-axis and the lines y = 1 and y = 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses vertical strips ∫₁⁴ x² dx = 21

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The area bounded by y² = 4x and x = 4 equals 2 × ∫₀⁴ 2√x dx.
Reason (R): The parabola y² = 4x is symmetric about the x-axis.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Symmetry means the lower half equals the upper half, so we double the upper integral (giving 64/3).
steps: R: y² = 4x is unchanged when y → −y, so it is symmetric about the x-axis — true
Lower half area = upper half area = ∫₀⁴ 2√x dx
So total = 2 × ∫₀⁴ 2√x dx: A is true because of R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Forgets the part of the region below the x-axis

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the area inside a parabola up to a line?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Solve for y, integrate one half up to the line, and double it by symmetry. Parabola done!
teach.nudge: Why can you integrate only one half and then double?

revise.summary: For a parabola and a line, use symmetry about the parabola's axis and choose the easier strips. In the first quadrant take only the positive branch, e.g. y = 2√x or x = 2√y.
focus: Area of y² = 4ax with x = k, and x² = 4ay with y = k
First-quadrant regions with horizontal strips
Use the right branch and limits
remember: Double the upper half for a region symmetric about the x-axis
traps: Don't forget the half below the x-axis when the region is symmetric
In the first quadrant, don't count both sides of the y-axis
Keep the coefficient, e.g. y = 3√x from y² = 9x

topics.title: Order and degree of a differential equation

learn.hook: Population growth, cooling chai, a swinging pendulum: each is described by an equation that involves a rate of change, a differential equation.
points: Differential equations model growth, decay, motion and many other changing quantities.

A differential equation involves derivatives of a dependent variable (y) with respect to an independent variable (x). If there is only one independent variable, it is an ordinary differential equation.
Order: the order of the highest derivative present.
Degree: when the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives, the power of the highest-order derivative (after clearing radicals and fractions in the derivatives).
Degree is not defined if a derivative appears inside a function like sin(y′), e^(y″) or log(y′). Order and degree (when defined) are always positive integers.

example.q: Find the order and degree of (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ + y = 0.
steps: The highest derivative is d²y/dx², so the order is 2.
The equation is a polynomial in the derivatives.
The power of d²y/dx² is 3, so the degree is 3.

learn.reallife: Newton's law of cooling, which describes how a cup of hot chai cools, dT/dt = −k(T − Tₛ), is a first-order, first-degree differential equation.

quiz.q: What is the order of y‴ + 2y″ + y′ = 0?
quiz.explain: The highest derivative is the third derivative y‴.
steps: Order = order of the highest derivative present
Derivatives present: y‴, y″, y′; highest is y‴ (third)
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of terms instead

quiz.q: What is the degree of (y‴)² + (y″)³ + (y′)⁴ + y⁵ = 0?
quiz.explain: The highest-order derivative is y‴ and its power is 2.
quiz.mistake: Takes the highest power anywhere in the equation

quiz.q: What is the degree of y″ + (y′)² + 2y = 0?
quiz.explain: The highest-order derivative y″ appears to the first power.
steps: It appears to the power 1 (the power 2 is on y′, a lower derivative)
quiz.mistake: Uses the power of y′ instead of the highest-order derivative

quiz.q: For y‴ + y² + e^(y′) = 0, which statement is correct?
quiz.explain: y‴ gives order 3. The term e^(y′) is not a polynomial in y′, so degree is not defined.
steps: Highest derivative is y‴, so order = 3
e^(y′) is not a polynomial in y′, so the equation is not a polynomial in its derivatives
quiz.mistake: Gives a degree even though a derivative sits inside an exponential

quiz.q: What is the degree of √(1 + (dy/dx)²) = d²y/dx² after removing the radical?
quiz.explain: Squaring: 1 + (dy/dx)² = (d²y/dx²)². The highest-order derivative has power 2.
quiz.mistake: Finds the degree before clearing the square root

quiz.q: What is the order of (dy/dx)⁴ + 3y (d²y/dx²) = 0?
quiz.explain: The highest derivative is d²y/dx², so the order is 2 (and the degree is 1).
steps: Highest is d²y/dx², so order = 2 (the power 4 of dy/dx is irrelevant to order)
quiz.mistake: Uses the power 4 of dy/dx as the order

quiz.q: Why is the degree of y″ + sin(y′) = 0 not defined?
options: Because the equation is not a polynomial in the derivatives
quiz.explain: Degree needs a polynomial form in y′, y″, …; sin(y′) is not a polynomial in y′.
steps: Degree is defined only when the equation is a polynomial in y′, y″, …
sin(y′) is not a polynomial in y′
Answer: Because the equation is not a polynomial in the derivatives
quiz.mistake: Thinks every differential equation has a degree

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The order of (dy/dx)⁵ + y = 0 is 5.
Reason (R): The degree of (dy/dx)⁵ + y = 0 is 5.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: The highest derivative is dy/dx, so the order is 1, and A is false. Its power is 5, so the degree is 5, and R is true.
steps: Only derivative present: dy/dx, so order = 1 ⇒ A (order 5) is false
dy/dx appears to the power 5, so degree = 5 ⇒ R is true
Answer: A is false but R is true
quiz.mistake: Mixes up order (which derivative) with degree (which power)

teach.ask: Gappu peeps: 'What is the difference between the order and the degree of a differential equation?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Order is the highest derivative; degree is its power, but only when the equation is a polynomial in derivatives!
teach.nudge: When can't we talk about the degree at all?

revise.summary: The order of a differential equation is the order of its highest derivative. The degree is the power of that derivative, defined only when the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives.
focus: Find order and degree of a given equation
Clear radicals before reading the degree
Spot equations whose degree is not defined
remember: Degree = power of the highest-order derivative (polynomial form only)
Degree not defined if a derivative is inside sin, e^, log etc.
traps: Don't use the highest power anywhere as the degree
Order is about which derivative, degree is about its power
Square away a radical before finding the degree

learn.hook: y = A cos x + B sin x solves y″ + y = 0 for every A and B. A whole family of curves, one equation. Pick A and B, and you get one particular member.
points: A solution of a differential equation is a function that satisfies it.
General solution: contains arbitrary constants. Particular solution: obtained by giving the constants definite values (no arbitrary constants left).
The number of arbitrary constants in the general solution equals the order of the equation.
To verify a solution: differentiate the given function as many times as needed, substitute into the equation, and check both sides match.
Forming a differential equation from a given general solution (eliminating constants) is not in the current CBSE syllabus.

example.q: Verify that y = eˣ + 1 is a solution of y″ − y′ = 0.
example.answer: Yes, y = eˣ + 1 satisfies y″ − y′ = 0.

learn.reallife: The equation of motion of a thrown cricket ball has a general solution that covers every possible throw; the release point and speed (the initial conditions) pick out one particular path.

games.title: Solution facts
items: The general solution of a second-order equation has two arbitrary constants.
A particular solution can contain arbitrary constants.
All constants are fixed in a particular solution.
y = A cos x + B sin x solves y″ + y = 0 for all A and B.
y″ = −A cos x − B sin x = −y.
Initial conditions are used to find particular solutions.
They fix the values of the constants.
A fourth-order equation's general solution has three constants.

quiz.q: How many arbitrary constants are in the general solution of a third-order differential equation?
quiz.explain: The number of arbitrary constants equals the order.
steps: Rule: number of arbitrary constants in the general solution = order
quiz.mistake: Confuses order with degree

quiz.q: How many arbitrary constants are there in a particular solution of a fourth-order differential equation?
quiz.explain: A particular solution has all its constants fixed, so it has none.
steps: A particular solution has every constant given a definite value
So no arbitrary constants remain, whatever the order
quiz.mistake: Confuses particular solution with general solution

quiz.q: Which function is a solution of y″ + y = 0?
quiz.explain: For y = 2 cos x − 3 sin x, y″ = −2 cos x + 3 sin x = −y.
steps: y = 2 cos x − 3 sin x: y′ = −2 sin x − 3 cos x, y″ = −2 cos x + 3 sin x = −y ✓
eˣ and e⁻ˣ give y″ = y; x² gives y″ = 2 ✗
Answer: y = 2 cos x − 3 sin x
quiz.mistake: Picks a function whose second derivative equals itself, not its negative

quiz.q: Which differential equation has y = √(1 + x²) as a solution?
steps: Multiply top and bottom by √(1 + x²): y′ = x√(1 + x²)/(1 + x²)
quiz.mistake: Differentiates without the chain rule

quiz.q: Which function is a solution of x dy/dx = y?
quiz.explain: y = Ax gives x · A = Ax = y.
steps: Try y = Ax: dy/dx = A, so x dy/dx = Ax = y ✓
y = Ax² gives 2Ax² ≠ y; y = A/x gives −A/x ≠ y
quiz.mistake: Checks only one value of x

quiz.q: y = x² + 2x + C is the general solution of which differential equation?
quiz.explain: Differentiating gives y′ = 2x + 2.
steps: Differentiate y = x² + 2x + C: y′ = 2x + 2 (C disappears)
quiz.mistake: Forgets to differentiate and matches the function itself

quiz.q: The general solution of y′ = 2x is y = x² + C. Which particular solution passes through (1, 4)?
quiz.explain: 4 = 1 + C gives C = 3.
quiz.mistake: Uses the y-value directly as C

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): y = A e^(2x) + B e^(−2x) is the general solution of y″ − 4y = 0.
Reason (R): It contains two arbitrary constants and satisfies the second-order equation.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: y″ = 4A e^(2x) + 4B e^(−2x) = 4y, and two constants match the order 2. R explains A.
steps: So it is the general solution, for exactly the reason R gives
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of constants does not matter

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the difference between a general solution and a particular solution?'
teach.praise: Chirp! General has arbitrary constants for a whole family; particular fixes them with conditions. One curve chosen!
teach.nudge: How do we turn a general solution into a particular one?

revise.summary: A general solution has as many arbitrary constants as the order, while a particular solution has none. To verify a solution, differentiate it and substitute into the equation.
focus: Count constants in general and particular solutions
Verify that a function satisfies an equation
Find a particular solution from a given point
remember: Number of arbitrary constants in general solution = order
traps: Don't confuse order with degree when counting constants
Don't take the y-value as C directly; substitute properly
y″ + y = 0 needs y″ = −y, not y″ = y

learn.hook: If dy/dx = g(x)h(y), you can put every y on one side and every x on the other, then integrate both. It is the first method every board paper tests.
points: Form: dy/dx = F(x, y) = g(x) h(y).
Separate: dy/h(y) = g(x) dx (with h(y) ≠ 0).
Integrate both sides: ∫dy/h(y) = ∫g(x) dx + C. That is the general solution.
For a particular solution, substitute the initial condition to find C.
Common results: dy/dx = ky gives y = Ae^(kx); dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²) gives tan⁻¹ y = tan⁻¹ x + C.

example.q: Find the particular solution of dy/dx = −4xy², given y = 1 when x = 0.

learn.reallife: Drug half-life calculations start from dC/dt = −kC, a variable separable equation whose solution is exponential decay.

quiz.q: What is the general solution of dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²)?
quiz.explain: dy/(1 + y²) = dx/(1 + x²); integrating both sides gives tan⁻¹ y = tan⁻¹ x + C.
steps: Integrate: ∫dy/(1 + y²) = tan⁻¹ y; ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹ x
Answer: tan⁻¹ y = tan⁻¹ x + C
quiz.mistake: Uses log instead of tan⁻¹

quiz.q: What is the general solution of dy/dx = e^(x + y)?
quiz.explain: e⁻ʸ dy = eˣ dx ⇒ −e⁻ʸ = eˣ + C₁ ⇒ eˣ + e⁻ʸ = C.
steps: e^(x + y) = eˣ eʸ ⇒ e⁻ʸ dy = eˣ dx
quiz.mistake: Loses the minus sign when integrating e⁻ʸ

quiz.q: For dy/dx = −4xy² with y(0) = 1, what is y at x = 1?
quiz.explain: The particular solution is y = 1/(2x² + 1), so y(1) = 1/3.
quiz.mistake: Uses 4x² instead of 2x²

quiz.q: What is the general solution of dy/dx = x/y?
quiz.explain: y dy = x dx ⇒ y²/2 = x²/2 + C₁ ⇒ y² − x² = C.
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip moving x² across

quiz.q: Which equation is variable separable?
quiz.explain: (x + 1)(y − 2) is a product of a function of x and a function of y.
steps: (x + 1)(y − 2) is a product of a function of x and a function of y ✓
x + y, (x + y)/(x − y) and x − y cannot be written as g(x)h(y)
quiz.mistake: Thinks any equation with x and y is separable

quiz.q: Solve dy/dx = y with y(0) = 2. What is y(1)?
quiz.explain: y = Aeˣ, A = 2, so y(1) = 2e.
steps: dy/y = dx ⇒ log|y| = x + c ⇒ y = Aeˣ
quiz.mistake: Forgets the constant A

quiz.q: What is the general solution of dy/dx = sin x/cos y?
quiz.explain: cos y dy = sin x dx ⇒ sin y = −cos x + C.
steps: Separate: cos y dy = sin x dx
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of ∫sin x dx wrong

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): dy/dx = 1 + x + y + xy is variable separable.
Reason (R): 1 + x + y + xy = (1 + x)(1 + y).
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The factorisation in R shows the right side is g(x)h(y), which is why the equation separates.
steps: So dy/dx = g(x)h(y) with g = 1 + x, h = 1 + y: separable
R is the reason A holds
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not try factorising before deciding

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I solve a variable separable differential equation?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Put y's with dy and x's with dx, integrate both sides, add + C, then use the condition. Separated and solved!
teach.nudge: After separating, what do you do to both sides?

revise.summary: If dy/dx = g(x)h(y), separate as dy/h(y) = g(x) dx and integrate both sides. Use an initial condition to find C for a particular solution.
focus: Recognise separable equations (factorise if needed)
Integrate both sides correctly
Find particular solutions
remember: dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²) ⇒ tan⁻¹ y = tan⁻¹ x + C
traps: Don't lose the minus sign in ∫e⁻ʸ dy = −e⁻ʸ
x + y is not separable; try factorising expressions like 1 + x + y + xy
Don't forget the constant A in y = Ae^(kx)

learn.hook: Money, microbes and mountains: compound interest, bacterial growth and the shape of a curve all fall to the same separate-and-integrate idea.
points: 'Rate proportional to amount' means dN/dt = kN, which gives N = N₀ e^(kt): growth if k > 0, decay if k < 0.
Continuous compounding at r% per year: dP/dt = (r/100)P, so P = P₀ e^(rt/100).
If a quantity grows by a fixed factor in a fixed time, use that to find k, e.g. doubling: e^(kT) = 2 ⇒ k = (log 2)/T.
A curve whose slope at (x, y) is given: write dy/dx = (given expression), solve, and use the given point to find C.
Always state what each variable means and include units in the final answer.

example.q: Find the curve through (−2, 3) whose slope at (x, y) is 2x/y².

learn.reallife: A fixed deposit with continuous compounding would grow by dP/dt = (r/100)P. Banks usually compound fixed deposits quarterly, but the continuous model is a close and simple estimate.

games.title: Bacteria doubling problem
items: Let N be the number at time t: dN/dt = kN
Separate and integrate: N = N₀ e^(kt)
Use the given data to find k
Set N equal to the target and solve for t

games.title: Growth model facts
items: If dN/dt = kN with k > 0, N grows exponentially.
N = N₀e^(kt) with k > 0 increases without bound.
Continuous compounding at 5% per year means dP/dt = 5P.
A quantity that doubles every T hours has k = (log 2)/T.
dN/dt = kN has the solution N = kt + C.
That would be the solution of dN/dt = k, a constant rate.
A slope condition plus one point gives one particular curve.

quiz.q: Money grows continuously at 5% per year. Which differential equation models the principal P?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert the percentage

quiz.q: For dP/dt = P/20 with P(0) = ₹1000, what is P after 20 years?
quiz.mistake: Uses simple interest instead

quiz.q: A bacteria culture doubles every 3 hours under dN/dt = kN. What is k?
steps: N = N₀ e^(kt); doubling in 3 h: N₀ e^(3k) = 2N₀
quiz.mistake: Inverts the relation

quiz.q: With N = N₀ e^(kt) and doubling every 3 hours, how many times larger is N after 9 hours?
quiz.explain: 9 hours is three doublings: 2³ = 8.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 2 by 3 instead of raising 2 to the power 3

quiz.q: A curve passes through (0, 1) and its slope at (x, y) is y. What is its equation?
quiz.explain: dy/dx = y ⇒ y = Aeˣ, and y(0) = 1 gives A = 1.
steps: dy/dx = y ⇒ dy/y = dx ⇒ y = Aeˣ
quiz.mistake: Treats slope y as a constant slope

quiz.q: For the curve through (−2, 3) with slope 2x/y², what is y³ when x = 1?
quiz.explain: y³ = 3x² + 15, so at x = 1, y³ = 18.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 3 multiplying x²

quiz.q: A population falls according to dN/dt = −kN (k > 0). Which graph shape fits?
quiz.explain: N = N₀e^(−kt) decreases and approaches 0 but never reaches it.
steps: e^(−kt) decreases and tends to 0 but never reaches it
Not a straight line: the fall slows down as N shrinks
quiz.mistake: Confuses exponential decay with a constant rate of fall

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In a bank paying continuous interest at r% per annum, P = P₀e^(rt/100).
Reason (R): The rate of growth of principal is proportional to the principal, dP/dt = (r/100)P.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Separating dP/P = (r/100) dt and integrating gives log P = rt/100 + C, which leads to A.
steps: R: dP/dt = (r/100)P — true for continuous interest
Separate: dP/P = (r/100) dt ⇒ log P = rt/100 + C ⇒ P = P₀ e^(rt/100)
So A follows by solving R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks continuous interest is linear

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How do I turn a word problem about growth into a differential equation?'
teach.praise: Chirp! 'Rate proportional to amount' means dN/dt = kN, which gives exponential growth. Use the data to find k!
teach.nudge: What does 'the rate is proportional to the amount' look like as an equation?

revise.summary: 'Rate proportional to amount' gives dN/dt = kN and N = N₀e^(kt): growth for k > 0 and decay for k < 0. Continuous interest follows P = P₀e^(rt/100), and slope problems give dy/dx directly.
focus: Model growth, decay and continuous interest
Find k from a doubling time
Find a curve from its slope and a point
traps: Convert r% to r/100
n doublings multiply by 2ⁿ, not 2n
Exponential decay is not a straight-line fall

learn.hook: dy/dx = (x + y)/x does not separate. But substitute y = vx and suddenly it does. That trick is the whole method.
points: F(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n if F(λx, λy) = λⁿ F(x, y) for all λ ≠ 0.
dy/dx = F(x, y) is homogeneous if F is homogeneous of degree 0, i.e. F(x, y) = g(y/x).
Method: put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. The equation becomes separable in v and x.
If dx/dy = G(x, y) with G of degree 0, put x = vy instead.
After integrating, replace v by y/x, then use any initial condition to find C.

example.q: Solve dy/dx = (x + y)/x.
steps: Degree 0: (λx + λy)/(λx) = (x + y)/x. Put y = vx.
v + x dv/dx = 1 + v ⇒ x dv/dx = 1 ⇒ dv = dx/x.
v = log|x| + C ⇒ y/x = log|x| + C.

learn.reallife: Homogeneous equations appear whenever a rate depends only on the direction y/x and not on the distance from the origin, for example in some curve-tracing and flow problems.

games.title: Solve (x² + y²) dx = 2xy dy
items: Put y = vx: v + x dv/dx = (1 + v²)/(2v)

quiz.q: What is the degree of the homogeneous function F(x, y) = x³ + 3x²y?
quiz.explain: F(λx, λy) = λ³(x³ + 3x²y), so the degree is 3.
steps: Replace x, y by λx, λy
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of terms

quiz.q: What is the degree of F(x, y) = (x³ + y³)/(x + y)?
quiz.explain: λ³/λ = λ², so the degree is 2.
quiz.mistake: Takes the degree of the numerator only

quiz.q: Which differential equation is homogeneous?
quiz.explain: (x² + y²)/(xy) is homogeneous of degree 0, so the equation is homogeneous.
steps: Homogeneous means the right side is homogeneous of degree 0
x + y + 1 and x² + y mix degrees; sin x + y is not homogeneous
quiz.mistake: Ignores the constant or mixed-degree terms

quiz.q: In a homogeneous equation, the substitution y = vx gives dy/dx =
quiz.explain: By the product rule, d(vx)/dx = v + x dv/dx.
steps: y = vx with v a function of x
Product rule: dy/dx = v · 1 + x · dv/dx
quiz.mistake: Forgets the product rule

quiz.q: What is the general solution of (x² + y²) dx = 2xy dy?
quiz.explain: With y = vx, 2v dv/(1 − v²) = dx/x gives (1 − v²)x = C, i.e. x² − y² = Cx.
steps: dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(2xy); put y = vx: v + x dv/dx = (1 + v²)/(2v)
x dv/dx = (1 − v²)/(2v) ⇒ 2v dv/(1 − v²) = dx/x
quiz.mistake: Drops the x on the right after replacing v

quiz.q: Solve dy/dx = (x + y)/x with y(1) = 1. Which is the particular solution?
quiz.explain: General: y = x log|x| + Cx. At x = 1: 1 = 0 + C, so C = 1.
steps: General solution (from the worked example): y = x log|x| + Cx
quiz.mistake: Forgets the Cx term

quiz.q: For dx/dy = (x + y)/y, which substitution is natural?
quiz.explain: When the equation is in the form dx/dy = G(x/y), use x = vy.
steps: The equation is dx/dy = (x + y)/y = x/y + 1, a function of x/y
For dx/dy = G(x/y), put x = vy
quiz.mistake: Always uses y = vx

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): dy/dx = (y/x) + tan(y/x) is homogeneous.
Reason (R): Its right side is a function of y/x alone.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: Any F(x, y) = g(y/x) is homogeneous of degree 0, which makes the equation homogeneous.
steps: R: right side = (y/x) + tan(y/x) is a function of y/x alone — true
Any g(y/x) is homogeneous of degree 0, so the equation is homogeneous
R is the reason A holds
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks trigonometric terms prevent homogeneity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is a homogeneous differential equation and how do I solve it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! If it depends only on y/x, put y = vx, separate the variables, and integrate. Homogeneous handled!
teach.nudge: Which substitution turns it into a separable equation?

revise.summary: dy/dx = F(x, y) is homogeneous when F is a function of y/x alone (degree 0). Put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, and the equation becomes separable.
focus: Find the degree of a homogeneous function
Check if an equation is homogeneous
Solve with y = vx (or x = vy)
remember: F(λx, λy) = λⁿF(x, y): degree n
y = vx ⇒ dy/dx = v + x dv/dx
For dx/dy = G(x/y), put x = vy
traps: Don't forget the product rule in d(vx)/dx
Mixed-degree terms or constants make it non-homogeneous
Replace v by y/x at the end

learn.hook: dy/dx + Py = Q: one magic multiplier, the integrating factor, turns the left side into the derivative of a single product.
points: Linear form: dy/dx + Py = Q, where P and Q are functions of x only (or constants).
Integrating factor IF = e^(∫P dx).
Solution: y · IF = ∫(Q · IF) dx + C.
If the equation is linear in x: dx/dy + P₁x = Q₁ (P₁, Q₁ functions of y), then IF = e^(∫P₁ dy) and x · IF = ∫(Q₁ · IF) dy + C.
Always rewrite into standard form first (divide by the coefficient of dy/dx).

example.q: Solve x dy/dx + 2y = x² (x ≠ 0).
steps: Standard form: dy/dx + (2/x)y = x. So P = 2/x, Q = x.
IF = e^(∫2/x dx) = e^(2 log x) = x².
y · x² = ∫x · x² dx = x⁴/4 + C.

learn.reallife: In electrical circuits, an inductor–resistor (RL) circuit obeys L di/dt + Ri = E, a linear equation solved with the same integrating factor.

games.title: Equation ↔ integrating factor
pairs: dy/dx + y tan x = sec x

games.title: Solve dy/dx + y tan x = sec x
items: P = tan x, Q = sec x
IF = e^(∫tan x dx) = sec x
y sec x = tan x + C
y = sin x + C cos x

quiz.q: What is the integrating factor of dy/dx + 3y = eˣ?
steps: Form dy/dx + Py = Q with P = 3, Q = eˣ
quiz.mistake: Uses Q instead of P

quiz.q: What is the integrating factor of x dy/dx − y = x² (x > 0)?
quiz.explain: Standard form: dy/dx − y/x = x, so P = −1/x and IF = e^(−log x) = 1/x.
steps: Divide by x: dy/dx − (1/x)y = x, so P = −1/x
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by x before reading P

quiz.q: What is the general solution of dy/dx + y/x = x² (x > 0)?
quiz.explain: IF = x. yx = ∫x³ dx = x⁴/4 + C ⇒ y = x³/4 + C/x.
steps: y · x = ∫x² · x dx = x⁴/4 + C
Divide by x: y = x³/4 + C/x
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide C by x

quiz.q: What is the general solution of dy/dx + y tan x = sec x?
options: y = sin x + C cos x
y = cos x + C sin x
y sec x = sec x + C
quiz.explain: IF = sec x; y sec x = tan x + C; multiply by cos x.
steps: P = tan x ⇒ IF = e^(log|sec x|) = sec x
y sec x = ∫sec x · sec x dx = tan x + C
Multiply by cos x: y = sin x + C cos x
Answer: y = sin x + C cos x
quiz.mistake: Uses log|sec x| itself as the IF

quiz.q: Solve dy/dx + 2y tan x = sin x, y = 0 at x = π/3. What is C in y = cos x + C cos²x?
quiz.explain: IF = sec²x; y sec²x = sec x + C ⇒ y = cos x + C cos²x. At π/3: 0 = 1/2 + C/4 ⇒ C = −2.
quiz.mistake: Makes a slip with cos²(π/3) = 1/4

quiz.q: For y dx − (x + 2y²) dy = 0, the equation is best written as
quiz.explain: y dx = (x + 2y²) dy ⇒ dx/dy = x/y + 2y ⇒ dx/dy − x/y = 2y, a linear equation in x.
steps: Move x/y to the left: dx/dy − x/y = 2y (linear in x)
quiz.mistake: Forces the equation into dy/dx form

quiz.q: Hence the general solution of y dx − (x + 2y²) dy = 0 is
quiz.explain: IF = e^(−∫dy/y) = 1/y. x/y = ∫2 dy = 2y + C ⇒ x = 2y² + Cy.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply C by y

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The integrating factor of dy/dx + Py = Q is e^(∫P dx).
Reason (R): Multiplying by e^(∫P dx) makes the left side the derivative of y · e^(∫P dx).
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: d/dx[y e^(∫P dx)] = e^(∫P dx)(dy/dx + Py), which is why this factor is chosen.
steps: R: d/dx[y e^(∫P dx)] = e^(∫P dx) dy/dx + y P e^(∫P dx) = e^(∫P dx)(dy/dx + Py) — true
So multiplying by e^(∫P dx) turns the left side into one derivative
That is why e^(∫P dx) is the IF: R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Memorises the IF without knowing why it works

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'How do I solve dy/dx + Py = Q?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Put it in standard form, IF = e^(∫P dx), then y · IF = ∫Q · IF dx + C. Linear solved!
teach.nudge: What is the formula for the integrating factor?

revise.summary: A linear equation dy/dx + Py = Q is solved with IF = e^(∫P dx), giving y · IF = ∫Q · IF dx + C. If it is linear in x, use dx/dy + P₁x = Q₁ instead.
focus: Write the equation in standard form
Find the integrating factor
Solve and apply initial conditions
remember: Linear in x: x · IF = ∫(Q₁ · IF) dy + C, IF = e^(∫P₁ dy)
traps: Divide by the coefficient of dy/dx before reading P
Divide C by the IF too
Use Q, not P, inside the integral, and P, not Q, in the IF

topics.title: Curves from slopes and choosing the method

learn.hook: In the exam, the hardest step is often deciding which method to use. A quick checklist turns panic into a plan.
points: Checklist: Can it be written as g(x) h(y)? Use separation. Is it a function of y/x only? Use y = vx. Is it dy/dx + Py = Q? Use the integrating factor.
Slope problems: 'slope at (x, y) is …' means dy/dx = … . Solve, then use the given point.
Example: the curve through the origin with slope x + y at (x, y) satisfies dy/dx − y = x.
Some equations fit more than one type; choose the easiest.
Always verify the final answer by substituting back if time allows.

example.q: Find the curve through the origin whose slope at every point (x, y) is x + y.
steps: dy/dx = x + y ⇒ dy/dx − y = x (linear, P = −1, Q = x).

learn.reallife: Weather forecasting models solve many differential equations together; recognising the type of each piece and picking the right method is a key skill there too.

games.title: Method check
items: dy/dx = x + y is variable separable.
x + y is not a product g(x)h(y).
dy/dx = y/x is both separable and homogeneous.
dy/y = dx/x, and y/x has degree 0.
dy/dx + y² = x is linear in y.
y² is not first degree in y.
The slope of the tangent is dy/dx.

quiz.q: Which method suits dy/dx = e^(x − y)?
quiz.explain: e^(x − y) = eˣ · e⁻ʸ, so eʸ dy = eˣ dx.
steps: e^(x − y) = eˣ · e⁻ʸ, a product g(x)h(y)
quiz.mistake: Does not split the exponential

quiz.q: Which method suits dy/dx − y/x = x²?
quiz.explain: It is in the form dy/dx + Py = Q with P = −1/x, Q = x².
steps: P = −1/x and Q = x² are functions of x only
x² stops it from being a function of y/x alone, so it is not homogeneous
quiz.mistake: Calls it homogeneous because of y/x

quiz.q: For the curve through the origin with slope x + y, what is y at x = 1?
quiz.explain: y = eˣ − x − 1, so y(1) = e − 2.
steps: Solution through the origin: y = eˣ − x − 1
quiz.mistake: Forgets the −x term

quiz.q: A curve has slope 2x at each point (x, y) and passes through (1, 3). What is y at x = 2?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the constant

quiz.q: A curve passes through (0, 2) and its slope at (x, y) is −y. What is y(0) · y′(0)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the negative sign in the slope

quiz.q: Which is the general solution of dy/dx = y/x?
quiz.explain: dy/y = dx/x ⇒ log|y| = log|x| + log|C| ⇒ y = Cx.
quiz.mistake: Mixes the logs and gets y = C/x

quiz.q: Solve dy/dx + y = eˣ. Which is the general solution?
quiz.explain: IF = eˣ. y eˣ = ∫e^(2x) dx = e^(2x)/2 + C ⇒ y = eˣ/2 + Ce⁻ˣ.
steps: y eˣ = ∫eˣ · eˣ dx = e^(2x)/2 + C
Divide by eˣ: y = eˣ/2 + Ce⁻ˣ
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide C by the IF

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): dy/dx = (x + y)² is a linear differential equation.
Reason (R): The right side contains y.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: (x + y)² contains y² terms, so the equation is not linear; A is false. R is true: the right side does contain y.
steps: Linear needs the form dy/dx + Py = Q, with y only to the first power
(x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y² contains y², so A is false
R: the right side does contain y — true
Answer: A is false but R is true
quiz.mistake: Thinks containing y makes an equation linear

teach.ask: Gappu is lost: 'Three methods! How do I choose which one to use?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Product of x-part and y-part: separate. Only y/x: homogeneous. dy/dx + Py = Q: integrating factor!
teach.nudge: What clue tells you to use the integrating factor?

revise.summary: Choose the method by the form: separable if it splits as g(x)h(y), homogeneous if it depends only on y/x, linear if it is dy/dx + Py = Q. Slope problems mean dy/dx equals the given expression.
focus: Pick the right method for an equation
Solve curve problems with a given point
Recognise when an equation is not linear
remember: Separable: g(x)h(y); homogeneous: g(y/x); linear: dy/dx + Py = Q
'Slope at (x, y) is f' means dy/dx = f
traps: dy/dx − y/x = x² is linear, not homogeneous
Terms like y² make an equation non-linear
Don't forget the constant before using the given point

topics.title: Vectors, position vectors and direction cosines

learn.hook: 'Go 5 km' is useless to a pilot. 'Go 5 km north-east' is an instruction. That difference between a scalar and a vector is where this chapter begins.
points: Scalars have magnitude only (mass, time, speed, temperature). Vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force).
A vector is a directed line segment AB with initial point A and terminal point B; its magnitude is the length |AB|.
Position vector of P(x, y, z): OP = xi + yj + zk, with |OP| = √(x² + y² + z²).
If OP makes angles α, β, γ with the x-, y-, z-axes, then l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ are its direction cosines, and l² + m² + n² = 1.
Direction ratios are any numbers a, b, c proportional to l, m, n; for r = ai + bj + ck, l = a/|r|, m = b/|r|, n = c/|r|.

example.q: Find the direction cosines of the vector i + 2j + 2k.

learn.reallife: Air traffic controllers at Delhi airport give each plane a velocity vector: speed plus heading. Two planes with the same speed but different headings are on very different paths.

quiz.q: What is the magnitude of the position vector of P(2, 3, −6)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root

quiz.q: What is the direction cosine n (with the z-axis) of the vector 2i − 2j + k?
quiz.mistake: Uses the component itself, forgetting to divide by |r|

quiz.q: A line makes angles 90°, 60° and γ with the x-, y- and z-axes. What is cos²γ?
quiz.explain: cos²90° + cos²60° + cos²γ = 1 ⇒ 0 + 1/4 + cos²γ = 1 ⇒ cos²γ = 3/4.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 60° instead of cos² 60°

quiz.q: Which are direction cosines of a vector equally inclined to the three axes?
quiz.explain: l = m = n and 3l² = 1, so l = 1/√3 (taking the positive sign).
quiz.mistake: Takes direction ratios 1, 1, 1 as direction cosines

quiz.q: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
quiz.explain: Work is a number (with units) with no direction; the others need a direction.
steps: Scalar: magnitude only; vector: magnitude and direction
Force, displacement and velocity all need a direction
Work done is just a number with units
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything in physics with units is a vector

quiz.q: Which set can be the direction ratios of a line with direction cosines 2/7, 3/7, 6/7?
quiz.explain: Direction ratios are proportional to direction cosines; 4, 6, 12 = 14 × (2/7, 3/7, 6/7).
steps: Direction ratios must be proportional to 2/7, 3/7, 6/7, in the same order
2, 3, 5 is not proportional; 6, 3, 2 is in the wrong order
quiz.mistake: Reorders the numbers, which changes the direction

quiz.q: For any vector, what is l² + m² + n²?
quiz.explain: This identity holds for every set of direction cosines.
steps: l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ for any direction
quiz.mistake: Confuses direction cosines with direction ratios

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): 1, 2, 2 are direction ratios but not direction cosines of a line.
Reason (R): For direction cosines, l² + m² + n² = 1.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 1 + 4 + 4 = 9 ≠ 1, so they cannot be direction cosines, but any proportional triple can be direction ratios.
steps: R: direction cosines satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1 — true
1² + 2² + 2² = 9 ≠ 1, so 1, 2, 2 are not direction cosines; but they can be direction ratios
So A is true, and R is the reason
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Treats direction ratios and cosines as the same

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'What makes a vector different from a plain number, and what are direction cosines?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A vector has size and direction; its direction cosines are cosines of the angles with the axes, and their squares add to 1!
teach.nudge: What special relation do l, m and n always satisfy?

revise.summary: A vector has magnitude and direction; the position vector of P(x, y, z) is xi + yj + zk with length √(x² + y² + z²). Its direction cosines l, m, n satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1.
focus: Find magnitude and direction cosines of a vector
Use l² + m² + n² = 1 to find a missing angle
Tell direction ratios from direction cosines
traps: Divide components by |r| to get direction cosines
Direction ratios need not satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1
Square the cosines: cos²60° = 1/4

learn.hook: Two cricket fielders running in the same direction at the same speed from different spots have equal velocity vectors, even though they start in different places.
points: Zero (null) vector 0: magnitude zero, initial and terminal points coincide; its direction is not defined (any direction).
Unit vector: magnitude 1; the unit vector along a is â. Coinitial vectors share the same initial point.
Collinear (parallel) vectors lie along the same or parallel lines, whatever their magnitudes or senses.
Equal vectors: same magnitude and same direction, regardless of initial points. Negative of AB is BA, with the same magnitude and opposite direction.
Free vectors can be moved parallel to themselves without change; in this chapter all vectors are free vectors.

example.q: In a square ABCD, classify AB and DC, and AB and CD.
steps: AB and DC have the same length and point the same way, so they are equal vectors.
CD points opposite to AB with the same length, so CD = −AB.
All of them are collinear (parallel) vectors.

learn.reallife: A map app's route is a chain of displacement vectors; sliding one leg of the route parallel to itself does not change that vector, because displacement vectors are free vectors.

games.title: Type check
items: Equal vectors must have the same initial point.
Two collinear vectors always have equal magnitudes.
Collinear vectors may differ in length.
i, j and k are unit vectors.
They have equal length and opposite directions.
The zero vector has a fixed direction.
They are parallel with the same sense.

quiz.q: Which vector is a unit vector?
quiz.mistake: Thinks a vector with entries 1 is automatically a unit vector

quiz.q: In parallelogram ABCD, which pair are equal vectors?
quiz.explain: Opposite sides AB and DC are equal in length and point the same way.
steps: Equal vectors: same length and same direction
In parallelogram ABCD, AB and DC are opposite sides pointing the same way
CD points the opposite way to AB, so CD = −AB
quiz.mistake: Confuses CD with DC

quiz.q: Vectors a and −3a are
quiz.explain: −3a is parallel to a (opposite sense, three times as long).
steps: −3a = (−3) × a: it lies along the same line as a
It is 3 times as long and points the opposite way, so it is not equal to a
quiz.mistake: Thinks opposite direction means not collinear

quiz.q: What is the magnitude of the zero vector?
quiz.explain: The zero vector has length zero.
steps: Zero vector: initial and terminal points coincide
quiz.mistake: Confuses magnitude with direction

quiz.q: Which statement about free vectors is true?
options: They must start at the origin
They can be shifted parallel to themselves without changing
quiz.explain: A free vector is defined only by magnitude and direction, not position.
steps: A free vector is fixed only by magnitude and direction
Its position does not matter, so it can be moved parallel to itself
Answer: They can be shifted parallel to themselves without changing
quiz.mistake: Mixes up free vectors with position vectors

quiz.q: Vectors OA, OB and OC all start at O. They are called
quiz.explain: Coinitial means having the same initial point.
steps: OA, OB, OC all have the same initial point O
Vectors with a common initial point are called coinitial
quiz.mistake: Assumes vectors with a common point must be collinear

quiz.q: Riya walks 4 km west, then 3 km north. What is the magnitude (km) of her displacement vector?
quiz.explain: The two legs are perpendicular, so the magnitude is √(16 + 9) = 5 km.
quiz.mistake: Adds the distances instead of combining the vectors

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two vectors having the same magnitude are equal.
Reason (R): Equal vectors have the same magnitude and the same direction.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Equality needs the same direction as well; i and j have the same magnitude but are not equal.
steps: R: equal vectors need the same magnitude and the same direction — true
i and j both have magnitude 1 but different directions, so they are not equal
Answer: A is false but R is true
quiz.mistake: Ignores direction when comparing vectors

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the difference between equal, collinear and negative vectors?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Equal: same size and direction. Collinear: parallel lines. Negative: same size, opposite direction!
teach.nudge: Can two vectors with the same length still be unequal?

revise.summary: Vectors may be zero, unit, coinitial, collinear, equal or negative of each other. Equal vectors need the same magnitude and the same direction; position does not matter for free vectors.
focus: Classify pairs of vectors in figures like parallelograms
Identify unit and zero vectors
Use perpendicular legs to find a displacement
remember: Equal vectors: same magnitude and direction
Collinear: along the same or parallel lines (any sense)
traps: Same magnitude alone does not make vectors equal
CD is not DC: CD = −DC
Opposite direction still counts as collinear

learn.hook: A boat crossing the Ganga while the river pushes it downstream ends up somewhere neither push alone would take it. Vector addition finds where.
points: Triangle law: if a and b are two sides of a triangle in order (head to tail), the third side taken from the start to the end is a + b: AB + BC = AC.
So AB + BC + CA = 0 for any triangle ABC.
Parallelogram law: if a and b are adjacent sides from a common point, the diagonal from that point is a + b.
Properties: a + b = b + a (commutative), (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) (associative), a + 0 = a, a + (−a) = 0.
Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|, with equality only when a and b point the same way.

example.q: In triangle ABC, simplify AB + BC + CA.
steps: By the triangle law, AB + BC = AC.

learn.reallife: Pilots flying from Mumbai to Chennai add the plane's air velocity to the wind velocity; the resultant vector is the actual ground track.

games.title: Triangle law
items: Draw vector a from point A to point B
Draw vector b starting at B, ending at C

quiz.q: In triangle ABC, what is AB + BC + CA?
quiz.explain: AB + BC = AC, and AC + CA = 0.
quiz.mistake: Adds magnitudes instead of vectors

quiz.q: In parallelogram ABCD, AB + AD equals
quiz.explain: By the parallelogram law, the diagonal from A is the sum of the adjacent sides from A.
steps: Parallelogram law: sum of adjacent sides from A = diagonal from A
AB + AD = AB + BC = AC (since AD = BC)
quiz.mistake: Picks the other diagonal

quiz.q: If |a| = 3 and |b| = 4, what is the greatest possible value of |a + b|?
quiz.explain: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b| = 7, with equality when a and b have the same direction.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the vectors are perpendicular

quiz.q: If |a| = 3 and |b| = 4, what is the least possible value of |a + b|?
quiz.explain: The sum is smallest when a and b point in opposite directions: 4 − 3 = 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sum can always be zero

quiz.q: Which property says (a + b) + c = a + (b + c)?
quiz.explain: Associativity means grouping does not matter.
steps: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c): the grouping changes, the order does not
That is the associative law (commutative is a + b = b + a)
quiz.mistake: Confuses associative with commutative

quiz.q: A boat moves at 4 km/h straight across a river flowing at 3 km/h. What is the boat's resultant speed (km/h)?
quiz.explain: The velocities are perpendicular, so |v| = √(16 + 9) = 5.
quiz.mistake: Adds the speeds directly

quiz.q: In triangle ABC, if AB = a and BC = b, then CA equals
quiz.explain: AB + BC + CA = 0, so CA = −(a + b).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For any two vectors, |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.
Reason (R): The length of any side of a triangle is at most the sum of the other two sides.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: a, b and a + b form a triangle (or a straight line), so A follows from the triangle side rule.
steps: R: a side of a triangle ≤ sum of the other two sides — true
a, b and a + b form a triangle (or lie on one line), with |a + b| as the third side
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks vector sums obey ordinary number addition for lengths

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I add two arrows?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Place them head to tail and join start to end, or use the parallelogram's diagonal. Arrow arithmetic!
teach.nudge: Where does the second arrow start in the triangle law?

revise.summary: Vectors add head to tail (triangle law) or along the diagonal of a parallelogram. Addition is commutative and associative, and |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.
focus: Simplify sums like AB + BC + CA
Use the parallelogram law
Find the largest and smallest possible |a + b|
remember: AB + BC = AC; AB + BC + CA = 0
traps: Don't add magnitudes when adding vectors
Least |a + b| is ||a| − |b||, not always 0
Keep the minus sign in CA = −(a + b)

learn.hook: Every vector in space is just a mix of three building blocks: i, j and k. Know the mix, and you know everything about the vector.
points: λa has magnitude |λ||a|; it points along a if λ > 0 and opposite if λ < 0. The unit vector along a is â = a/|a|.
r = xi + yj + zk: x, y, z are scalar components and xi, yj, zk are vector components.
Operations are componentwise; a = b exactly when corresponding components are equal.
a and b are collinear ⇔ b = λa for some scalar λ ⇔ their components are proportional.
Vector joining P(x₁, y₁, z₁) to Q(x₂, y₂, z₂): PQ = (x₂ − x₁)i + (y₂ − y₁)j + (z₂ − z₁)k.

example.q: Find a vector of magnitude 14 in the direction of 2i − 3j + 6k.

learn.reallife: A delivery drone's flight can be described leg by leg with components east, north and up; adding the components gives the drone's net position.

items.q: x-component of PQ for P(2, 3, 0), Q(−1, −2, −4)
x if xi + 2j − zk = 3i + yj + k
z if xi + 2j − zk = 3i + yj + k

games.title: Collinear or not?
items: The second is −2 times the first.
i + j and i − j are collinear.
−a has the same magnitude as a.
a/|a| is a unit vector for every non-zero a.

quiz.q: Find the unit vector in the direction of a = 2i + 3j + k.
quiz.mistake: Divides by |a|² instead of |a|

quiz.q: P(2, 3, 0) and Q(−1, −2, −4). What is PQ?
steps: PQ = OQ − OP = (x₂ − x₁)i + (y₂ − y₁)j + (z₂ − z₁)k
quiz.mistake: Subtracts Q from P instead of P from Q

quiz.q: Find a vector of magnitude 21 in the direction of 2i − 3j + 6k.
quiz.explain: |2i − 3j + 6k| = 7, so multiply the unit vector by 21: 3(2i − 3j + 6k).
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the vector itself by 21

quiz.q: If a = 2i − 3j + 4k and b = −4i + λj − 8k are collinear, what is λ?
quiz.explain: b = −2a requires λ = −2 × (−3) = 6.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign wrong

quiz.q: If xi + 2j − zk = 3i + yj + k, what is x + y + z?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign on z

quiz.q: Show A(1, 2, 7), B(2, 6, 3), C(3, 10, −1) are collinear. Which fact proves it?
options: A, B, C have positive x-coordinates
quiz.explain: AB and BC are parallel and share point B, so A, B, C lie on one line.
steps: AB = BC, so AC = AB + BC = 2AB; parallel with common point B ⇒ collinear
Answer: AB = BC = i + 4j − 4k, so AC = 2AB
quiz.mistake: Uses equal magnitudes, which does not show the same line

quiz.q: What are the scalar components of the vector joining A(1, −1, 2) to B(4, 3, 2)?
quiz.explain: AB = (4 − 1)i + (3 + 1)j + (2 − 2)k = 3i + 4j. Scalar components are 3, 4, 0.
quiz.mistake: Gives vector components when scalar components were asked

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): −2a is a vector of magnitude 2|a| opposite to a.
Reason (R): For a scalar λ, |λa| = |λ||a|, and λa reverses direction when λ < 0.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With λ = −2, |λa| = 2|a| and the direction reverses.
steps: R: |λa| = |λ||a|, and λ < 0 reverses direction — true
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative scalar makes the magnitude negative

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find a vector of length 14 pointing the same way as 2i − 3j + 6k?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Divide by its magnitude to get the unit vector, then multiply by 14. Same direction, new length!
teach.nudge: What do you first divide the vector by?

revise.summary: λa scales the length by |λ| and reverses direction when λ < 0. Vectors are added, compared and scaled componentwise, and two vectors are collinear exactly when their components are proportional.
focus: Find a unit vector and a vector of given magnitude
Find PQ from two points
Test collinearity by proportional components
traps: Subtract P from Q for PQ, not Q from P
Scalar components are numbers; vector components include i, j, k
Multiply the unit vector, not the vector, by the required magnitude

learn.hook: Where exactly is the point two-thirds of the way from Pune to Mumbai on a straight road? The section formula answers instantly in vector form.
points: If P and Q have position vectors a and b, the point R dividing PQ internally in the ratio m : n has position vector (mb + na)/(m + n).
Externally in the ratio m : n (m ≠ n): (mb − na)/(m − n).
Mid-point of PQ: (a + b)/2 (internal division with m = n = 1).
Centroid of a triangle with vertices a, b, c: (a + b + c)/3.
Remember the 'cross' pattern: m goes with b (the far end), n with a (the near end).
