example.q: OP = i + 2j − k and OQ = −i + j + k. Find the point R dividing PQ internally in the ratio 2 : 1.

learn.reallife: To place a station two-thirds of the way along a straight stretch of track between two points, a planner can use exactly this section formula.

games.title: External division of PQ in 2 : 1 (P = i + 2j − k, Q = −i + j + k)

quiz.q: What is the position vector of the mid-point of a and b?
quiz.explain: Internal division with m = n = 1 gives (a + b)/2.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adding

quiz.q: P = i + 2j − k and Q = −i + j + k. R divides PQ externally in the ratio 2 : 1. What is OR?
steps: External: OR = (m OQ − n OP)/(m − n) with m = 2, n = 1
quiz.mistake: Uses the internal formula instead

quiz.q: A has position vector 2i + j − k and B has 4i − 3j + 5k. What is the x-component of the mid-point of AB?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2

quiz.q: Find the position vector of the point dividing a = 2i + j and b = 5i + 7j internally in 1 : 2. What is its y-component?
quiz.mistake: Pairs m with a instead of b

quiz.q: The centroid of the triangle with vertices i, j and k has position vector
quiz.explain: Centroid = (a + b + c)/3.
steps: a = i, b = j, c = k
quiz.mistake: Uses 1/2 as for a mid-point

quiz.q: In the internal section formula (mb + na)/(m + n), which ratio does R divide PQ in, with P at a and Q at b?
quiz.explain: R is closer to P when m < n; the weights cross over to the far end.
steps: In (mb + na)/(m + n), m is the weight on b (the end Q) and n on a (the end P)
This gives the point R with PR : RQ = m : n
quiz.mistake: Reverses the meaning of the ratio

quiz.q: For external division in the ratio 3 : 1 of a = i and b = 2i, what is the resulting vector?
quiz.mistake: Uses m + n in the denominator

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The mid-point formula is a special case of the internal section formula.
Reason (R): Taking m = n = 1 in (mb + na)/(m + n) gives (a + b)/2.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Equal ratio 1 : 1 gives the mid-point, which R computes.
steps: R: m = n = 1 in (mb + na)/(m + n) gives (b + a)/2 — true
So the mid-point formula comes from the section formula: A is true because of R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Treats the mid-point formula as unrelated

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the point dividing a line segment in the ratio m : n using vectors?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Internal: (mb + na)/(m + n). External: (mb − na)/(m − n). Cross the weights and divide!
teach.nudge: Which position vector does m multiply, a or b?

revise.summary: The point dividing PQ internally in m : n is (mb + na)/(m + n), and externally (mb − na)/(m − n). The mid-point is (a + b)/2 and the centroid is (a + b + c)/3.
focus: Apply internal and external section formulas
Find mid-points and centroids
Pair m with the far end b
traps: Don't pair m with a
Use m − n, not m + n, for external division
Centroid uses 1/3, not 1/2

learn.hook: Pull a cart with a rope at an angle and only part of your force moves it forward. The dot product measures exactly that useful part.
points: a · b = |a||b| cos θ, where θ (0 ≤ θ ≤ π) is the angle between a and b. The result is a scalar.
Properties: a · b = b · a, a · (b + c) = a · b + a · c, (λa) · b = λ(a · b).
i · i = j · j = k · k = 1 and i · j = j · k = k · i = 0. So (a₁i + a₂j + a₃k) · (b₁i + b₂j + b₃k) = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.
Angle: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).
a ⊥ b ⇔ a · b = 0 (for non-zero vectors). a · a = |a|².

example.q: Find the angle between a = i + j and b = j + k.

learn.reallife: In physics, work = F · d. A porter at a railway station carrying luggage horizontally does no work against gravity, since force and displacement are perpendicular.

games.title: Dot product facts
items: If a · b = 0 for non-zero a, b, they are perpendicular.
i and j are perpendicular, so i · j = 0.
If a · b < 0, the angle between them is obtuse.
cos θ < 0 means θ is between π/2 and π.

quiz.q: Find (2i + 3j + k) · (i − j + 2k).
quiz.mistake: Drops a sign

quiz.q: For which λ are 2i + λj + k and i − 2j + 3k perpendicular?
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip solving 5 − 2λ = 0

quiz.q: Find cos θ for the angle between i − 2j + 3k and 3i − 2j + k.
quiz.explain: Dot = 3 + 4 + 3 = 10, each magnitude √14, cos θ = 10/14 = 5/7.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that (−2)(−2) = +4

quiz.q: |a| = √3, |b| = 2 and a · b = √6. What is the angle between a and b?
quiz.mistake: Simplifies √6/√3 wrongly

quiz.q: What is i · (j × k)?
quiz.explain: j × k = i, and i · i = 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every product of different unit vectors is 0

quiz.q: If a · b = 0 and a, b are non-zero, what is the angle between them?
quiz.explain: cos θ = 0 gives θ = π/2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a zero dot product means parallel vectors

quiz.q: Which pair of vectors is perpendicular?
options: i + j − k and 2i − j + k
steps: Answer: i + j − k and 2i − j + k
quiz.mistake: Checks only two components

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For non-zero vectors, a · b = |a||b| exactly when a and b point in the same direction.
Reason (R): cos θ = 1 only when θ = 0.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: a · b = |a||b| cos θ equals |a||b| only if cos θ = 1, i.e. θ = 0.
steps: a · b = |a||b| ⇔ cos θ = 1 ⇔ θ = 0 (R, true for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π)
θ = 0 means same direction, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the dot product equals the product of magnitudes for any angle

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the angle between two vectors?'
teach.praise: Chirp! cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Multiply matching components, add, divide by the lengths!
teach.nudge: Which formula links the dot product with the angle?

revise.summary: a · b = |a||b| cos θ is a scalar, and in components it is a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃. Non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when a · b = 0.
focus: Compute dot products in components
Find the angle between two vectors
Find an unknown that makes vectors perpendicular
remember: a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃
i · i = 1, i · j = 0; a · a = |a|²
traps: (−2)(−2) = +4: watch signs
A zero dot product means perpendicular, not parallel
The dot product is a number, not a vector

learn.hook: A wind of 20 km/h blows at an angle to a runway. How much of it is a headwind? That is the projection of the wind vector on the runway.
points: Projection of a on b = (a · b)/|b| = a · b̂. Its vector form is ((a · b)/|b|²) b.
The projection is positive if the angle is acute and negative if obtuse.
|a + b|² = |a|² + 2a · b + |b|², |a − b|² = |a|² − 2a · b + |b|², and (a + b) · (a − b) = |a|² − |b|².
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: |a · b| ≤ |a||b|. Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.
If |a + b| = |a − b|, then a · b = 0, so a ⊥ b.

example.q: Find the projection of a = 2i + 3j + 2k on b = i + 2j + k.

learn.reallife: Cricket analysts break a ball's velocity into a part along the pitch and a part across it; the along-pitch part is a projection.

items.q: Projection of i + j on j

quiz.q: Find the projection of a = 3i + 4j on b = i.
quiz.explain: a · b = 3 and |b| = 1, so the projection is 3.
quiz.mistake: Takes the magnitude of a instead

quiz.q: Find the projection of i + 3j + 7k on 7i − j + 8k.
steps: Projection of a on b = (a · b)/|b|
quiz.mistake: Divides by |a| instead of |b|

quiz.q: |a| = 2, |b| = 3 and a · b = 4. What is |a − b|²?
quiz.mistake: Adds 2a · b instead of subtracting

quiz.q: If a is a unit vector and (x − a) · (x + a) = 8, what is |x|?
quiz.mistake: Forgets |a|² = 1 or stops at |x|² = 9

quiz.q: If |a + b| = |a − b|, what is the angle between a and b (non-zero)?
quiz.explain: Squaring: |a|² + 2a · b + |b|² = |a|² − 2a · b + |b|², so a · b = 0.
steps: Non-zero vectors with zero dot product are perpendicular
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal magnitudes mean equal vectors

quiz.q: a, b, c are unit vectors with a + b + c = 0. What is a · b + b · c + c · a?
quiz.explain: |a + b + c|² = 3 + 2(a · b + b · c + c · a) = 0, so the sum is −3/2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that each |a|² = 1

quiz.q: Expand (3a − 5b) · (2a + 7b).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the cross terms or their signs

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): |a · b| ≤ |a||b| for all vectors a and b.
Reason (R): |cos θ| ≤ 1 for every angle θ.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: |a · b| = |a||b||cos θ| ≤ |a||b| because |cos θ| ≤ 1.
steps: a · b = |a||b| cos θ ⇒ |a · b| = |a||b||cos θ|
So |a · b| ≤ |a||b|: A follows from R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the inequality to the cosine bound

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does the projection of one vector on another mean?'
teach.praise: Tweet! It is the shadow of a along b: (a · b)/|b|. Dot, then divide by b's length!
teach.nudge: What do you divide a · b by?

revise.summary: The projection of a on b is (a · b)/|b|. Expansions like |a ± b|² = |a|² ± 2a · b + |b|² and (a + b) · (a − b) = |a|² − |b|² solve many magnitude problems.
focus: Find the projection of one vector on another
Use dot product identities to find magnitudes
Handle a + b + c = 0 type problems
remember: Projection of a on b = (a · b)/|b|
traps: Divide by |b| (the vector projected on), not |a|
Take the square root at the end when |x| is asked
Don't forget cross terms when expanding

learn.hook: Tighten a bolt with a spanner: the turning effect points along the bolt, perpendicular to both the spanner and your push. That direction is a cross product.
points: a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂, where n̂ is the unit vector perpendicular to both, chosen by the right-hand rule. The result is a vector.
Anti-commutative: a × b = −(b × a). Distributive: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c. a × a = 0.
i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j; and j × i = −k, k × j = −i, i × k = −j; i × i = j × j = k × k = 0.
Component form: a × b = |i j k; a₁ a₂ a₃; b₁ b₂ b₃| (a 3 × 3 determinant).
Non-zero a and b are parallel ⇔ a × b = 0. (The scalar triple product is not in the current CBSE syllabus.)

example.q: Find (i − 7j + 7k) × (3i − 2j + 2k).

learn.reallife: Torque τ = r × F decides how a wind turbine in Tamil Nadu's Muppandal wind farm spins: only the force component perpendicular to the blade turns it.

games.title: Cross product facts
items: a × b is perpendicular to both a and b.
It points along n̂, normal to their plane.
If a × b = 0 for non-zero a, b, they are perpendicular.
The cross product of two vectors is a scalar.

quiz.q: Find (i + j + k) × (i + 2j + 3k).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign on the j term

quiz.q: What is |(i − 7j + 7k) × (3i − 2j + 2k)|?
quiz.explain: The cross product is 19j + 19k, magnitude √(361 + 361) = 19√2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the components instead of using √(sum of squares)

quiz.q: |a| = 10, |b| = 2 and a · b = 12. What is |a × b|?
quiz.mistake: Uses cos θ instead of sin θ

quiz.q: If (2i + 6j + 27k) × (i + λj + μk) = 0, what is λ?
quiz.explain: Parallel vectors have proportional components: 2/1 = 6/λ = 27/μ, so λ = 3 (and μ = 27/2).
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: For the same equation (2i + 6j + 27k) × (i + λj + μk) = 0, what is μ?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 27 by 2 instead of dividing

quiz.q: What is k × j?
quiz.explain: j × k = i, so k × j = −i.
steps: Swapping the order changes the sign: k × j = −(j × k)
quiz.mistake: Ignores the order in a cross product

quiz.q: |a| = 2, |b| = 3 and a · b = 3. What is |a × b|²?
quiz.mistake: Adds (a · b)² instead of subtracting

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): a × b = −(b × a).
Reason (R): Swapping a and b reverses the right-hand-rule direction while keeping |a||b| sin θ the same.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Same magnitude, opposite normal direction: so b × a = −(a × b).
steps: |b × a| = |b||a| sin θ = |a × b|: same magnitude
Right-hand rule from b to a gives the opposite normal direction
So b × a = −(a × b): R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cross product is commutative like the dot product

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'How is the cross product different from the dot product?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The cross product is a vector perpendicular to both, with size |a||b| sin θ, found by the i j k determinant!
teach.nudge: Is a × b a number or a vector, and which way does it point?

revise.summary: a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂ is a vector perpendicular to both a and b, found by a 3 × 3 determinant. It is anti-commutative, and non-zero vectors are parallel exactly when a × b = 0.
focus: Compute a × b by the determinant
Use |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ
Find unknowns from a × b = 0
remember: i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j; reversed order gives the negative
traps: Don't forget the minus on the j term of the determinant
Use sin θ, not cos θ, for |a × b|
k × j = −i, not i

topics.title: Using the cross product: perpendicular vectors and areas

learn.hook: Need the area of a triangular plot from three GPS points in 3D? One cross product and a half do it.
points: A unit vector perpendicular to both a and b: ±(a × b)/|a × b|.
Area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides a and b: |a × b|.
Area of a triangle with sides a and b from one vertex: (1/2)|a × b|.

topics.title: Direction cosines and direction ratios of a line

learn.hook: A drone climbs from a rooftop in Bengaluru towards a tower. Three numbers, its direction cosines, pin down that heading in 3D space.
points: Vector algebra lets us describe lines in space neatly. If a line makes angles α, β, γ with the x-, y-, z-axes, its direction cosines are l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ.
Direction ratios a, b, c are any numbers proportional to l, m, n. A line has infinitely many sets of direction ratios.
From direction ratios: l = a/√(a² + b² + c²), m = b/√(…), n = c/√(…) (or all with the opposite sign).
Line through P(x₁, y₁, z₁) and Q(x₂, y₂, z₂): direction ratios x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁; divide by PQ for direction cosines.
Three points are collinear if the direction ratios of AB and BC are proportional. (The derivation of l² + m² + n² = 1 is not in the current syllabus; the result is used.)

example.q: Find the direction cosines of the line through P(−2, 4, −5) and Q(1, 2, 3).

learn.reallife: If GPS gives the coordinates of a base camp and of a ledge above it, the differences of the coordinates are direction ratios of the straight rope line between them; any proportional set describes the same line.

topics.title: Equation of a line in space

learn.hook: One point and one direction: that is all you need to describe a straight line in space, whether it is a laser beam or a metro tunnel.
points: Vector form: a line through the point with position vector a, parallel to b, is r = a + λb (λ a real parameter).
Cartesian form: through (x₁, y₁, z₁) with direction ratios a, b, c: (x − x₁)/a = (y − y₁)/b = (z − z₁)/c.

A line parallel to a given line has the same direction ratios.

With direction cosines, cos θ = |l₁l₂ + m₁m₂ + n₁n₂|.

learn.hook: Two flyovers cross at different heights without meeting. How close do they get? That gap is the shortest distance between skew lines.
points: Skew lines are lines in space that are neither parallel nor intersecting (they lie in different planes).
The shortest distance is along the segment perpendicular to both lines.
For r = a₁ + λb₁ and r = a₂ + μb₂: d = |(a₂ − a₁) · (b₁ × b₂)| / |b₁ × b₂|.

If d = 0, the lines intersect.

No, they pass through different points

quiz.mistake: Thinks the lines meet

Find a line through a point perpendicular to two lines
Recognise parallel lines from proportional directions

topics.title: What is a linear programming problem?

learn.hook: A furniture dealer in Jodhpur has limited money and limited space. How many tables and chairs should he stock to earn the most? That is a linear programming problem.
points: Linear programming finds the maximum (profit) or minimum (cost) of a linear function under linear restrictions.
Decision variables (x, y) are the quantities we choose. Usually x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (non-negative restrictions).
Objective function: Z = ax + by, to be maximised or minimised.
Constraints: linear inequalities (≤ or ≥) that the variables must satisfy.
Formulating: define variables, write Z, translate each condition into an inequality. (The 'different types of LPP' section is not in the current syllabus.)

example.q: A dealer buys tables at ₹2500 and chairs at ₹500, with ₹50,000 to spend and space for 60 pieces. Profit is ₹250 per table and ₹75 per chair. Formulate the LPP.
example.answer: Maximise Z = 250x + 75y subject to 5x + y ≤ 100, x + y ≤ 60, x, y ≥ 0

learn.reallife: Oil refineries use linear programming to decide how much petrol, diesel and LPG to produce from crude oil so that profit is as large as possible within the plant's limits.

games.title: Formulate an LPP
items: Translate each condition into an inequality

quiz.q: In 'Maximise Z = 3x + 4y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x, y ≥ 0', what is Z called?
quiz.explain: Z is the linear function to be optimised.
steps: Z = 3x + 4y is the linear function we want to maximise
x + y ≤ 4 and x, y ≥ 0 are the constraints; x, y are decision variables
quiz.mistake: Confuses the objective with the constraints

quiz.q: Each table needs 3 hours and each chair 1 hour of carpentry; 30 hours are available. Which constraint is correct (x tables, y chairs)?
quiz.explain: Total hours used, 3x + y, cannot exceed 30.
steps: Hours used: 3 per table × x tables + 1 per chair × y chairs = 3x + y
quiz.mistake: Attaches the 3 hours to the wrong variable

quiz.q: A diet needs at least 8 units of vitamin A. Food P gives 2 units per kg and food Q gives 1 unit per kg. Which constraint fits?
quiz.explain: 'At least' means ≥, and P (x kg) gives 2x while Q (y kg) gives y.
steps: Vitamin A supplied: 2 per kg × x + 1 per kg × y = 2x + y
quiz.mistake: Uses ≤ for 'at least'

quiz.q: Why are x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 included in most LPPs?
options: Quantities like numbers of items cannot be negative
quiz.explain: Decision variables represent real quantities that cannot be negative.
steps: Decision variables count real things (items, kg, hours)
Answer: Quantities like numbers of items cannot be negative
quiz.mistake: Thinks they are needed only to simplify graphs

quiz.q: For the furniture dealer, the budget condition 2500x + 500y ≤ 50000 simplifies to
quiz.explain: Divide by 500: 5x + y ≤ 100.
quiz.mistake: Divides only some terms

quiz.q: A factory makes x units of A (profit ₹40 each) and y units of B (profit ₹30 each). What is the objective function?
quiz.explain: Profit is to be maximised: Z = 40x + 30y.
steps: Profit is to be made as large as possible: maximise
quiz.mistake: Swaps the coefficients or chooses minimise for profit

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a linear constraint?
quiz.explain: xy is a product of variables, so it is not linear.
steps: Linear: each variable appears only to the first power, with no products
2x + 3y ≤ 12, x ≥ 0 and x − y ≥ −1 are linear
xy is a product of two variables, so it is not linear
quiz.mistake: Thinks any inequality is linear

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The objective function of an LPP is always a linear function of the decision variables.
Reason (R): In linear programming, the objective and all constraints are linear.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Linearity of the objective is part of the definition of an LPP, stated by R.
steps: R: in an LPP the objective and every constraint are linear — true (definition)
So the objective is always linear: A follows from R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks only constraints need to be linear

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What are the parts of a linear programming problem?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Decision variables, an objective to maximise or minimise, and linear constraints including non-negativity. LPP assembled!
teach.nudge: What do we call the inequalities the variables must obey?

revise.summary: A linear programming problem maximises or minimises a linear objective Z = ax + by subject to linear constraints, usually with x, y ≥ 0. Formulating means naming the variables, writing Z and turning each condition into an inequality.
focus: Identify objective, constraints and decision variables
Translate word conditions into inequalities
Simplify constraints by dividing through
remember: Objective: Z = ax + by (maximise or minimise)
traps: Attach each coefficient to the right variable
Products like xy are not linear
Profit is maximised, cost is minimised

topics.title: Graphing constraints and the feasible region

learn.hook: Each constraint cuts the plane in half. Overlap all the allowed halves and you get the feasible region: the only places the answer can live.
points: Each linear inequality ax + by ≤ c represents a half-plane bounded by the line ax + by = c.
To shade the correct side, test a point not on the line (often the origin).
The feasible region is the common region of all constraints (including x, y ≥ 0). Points in it are feasible solutions; points outside are infeasible.
An optimal (feasible) solution is a feasible point that gives the best value of Z.
The corner points of the feasible region are the intersections of its boundary lines.

example.q: Find the corner points of the region x + y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 90, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
steps: x + y = 50 meets the axes at (50, 0) and (0, 50); 3x + y = 90 at (30, 0) and (0, 90).
The origin satisfies both, so shade towards it.
Intersection: subtract the equations: 2x = 40, x = 20, y = 30.

learn.reallife: A spice exporter can plot weight and budget limits as lines; the overlap of the allowed regions shows every possible shipment mix.

games.title: Is the point feasible for x + y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 90, x, y ≥ 0?
Draw the feasible region
items: Draw each boundary line from its intercepts
Test the origin in each inequality
Shade the correct half-plane for each constraint
Take the common region in the first quadrant

quiz.q: Which side of the line 2x + 3y = 12 does 2x + 3y ≤ 12 represent?
options: The side away from the origin
quiz.explain: At (0, 0), 0 ≤ 12 is true, so the half-plane containing the origin is shaded.
steps: The origin satisfies it, so shade the side containing the origin
Answer: The side containing the origin
quiz.mistake: Shades the wrong side without testing a point

quiz.q: What is the intersection point of x + y = 50 and 3x + y = 90?
quiz.explain: Subtracting: 2x = 40 ⇒ x = 20, then y = 30.
quiz.mistake: Swaps x and y

quiz.q: Is (30, 10) a feasible point for x + y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 90, x, y ≥ 0?
options: Yes, because both coordinates are positive
quiz.explain: It satisfies the first constraint but breaks the second, so it is infeasible.
steps: One broken constraint makes it infeasible
quiz.mistake: Checks only one constraint

quiz.q: For x + 2y ≥ 10 and 3x + 4y ≤ 24 with x, y ≥ 0, which corner is the intersection of the two lines?
quiz.mistake: Solves the system with a sign slip

quiz.q: What is the y-intercept of the boundary line 3x + 4y = 24?
quiz.mistake: Gives the x-intercept instead

quiz.q: What is a feasible solution of an LPP?
options: Any point that satisfies all the constraints
quiz.explain: Feasible means allowed by every constraint; optimal means best among them.
steps: Feasible = satisfies every constraint (including x, y ≥ 0)
Optimal = the feasible point giving the best Z; corners are only special feasible points
Answer: Any point that satisfies all the constraints
quiz.mistake: Confuses feasible with optimal

quiz.q: How many corner points does the region x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 have?
quiz.explain: It is a triangle with corners (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 4).
steps: x + y = 4 meets the axes at (4, 0) and (0, 4)
With x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 the region is a triangle
quiz.mistake: Counts the intercepts only

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The point (2, 2) lies in the feasible region of x + y ≤ 5, x − y ≥ 1, x, y ≥ 0.
Reason (R): 2 + 2 ≤ 5.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: x − y = 0, which is not ≥ 1, so (2, 2) is infeasible. R is true but checks only one constraint.
steps: But x − y = 2 − 2 = 0, and 0 ≥ 1 is false
So (2, 2) is not feasible: A is false
Answer: A is false but R is true
quiz.mistake: Checks only one of the constraints

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the feasible region of an LPP?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Draw each line, test the origin to shade the right side, and the overlap is the feasible region!
teach.nudge: How do you decide which side of a line to shade?

revise.summary: Each linear inequality is a half-plane; test a point such as the origin to choose the side. The feasible region is where all constraints overlap, and its corners are where boundary lines meet.
focus: Shade half-planes correctly
Find corner points by solving boundary equations
Test whether a point is feasible
remember: Test the origin to decide which side to shade
Corner point: intersection of two boundary lines of the region
traps: Check every constraint, not just one, for feasibility
Feasible is not the same as optimal
Don't swap x and y when solving for a corner

learn.hook: Among infinitely many feasible points, the best one is always at a corner. So you only need to check a handful of points.
points: Theorem 1: if an LPP has an optimal value, it occurs at a corner point of the feasible region.
Theorem 2: if the feasible region is bounded, Z has both a maximum and a minimum, each at a corner point.
Corner point method: (1) draw the feasible region and find its corners, (2) evaluate Z at each corner, (3) pick the largest (max) or smallest (min) if the region is bounded.
Organise the work in a table: corner point | value of Z.
Always state the answer with the point and the value, e.g. 'maximum Z = 120 at (30, 0)'.

example.q: Maximise Z = 4x + y subject to x + y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 90, x, y ≥ 0.
steps: The region is bounded, so the maximum is the largest value.

learn.reallife: A factory planning how many units of two products to make uses the same corner principle: with a linear profit and linear limits, the best plan sits at a corner of the feasible region.

games.title: Corner point method
items: Choose the largest or smallest value
State the optimal point and value

quiz.q: Maximise Z = 4x + y subject to x + y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 90, x, y ≥ 0. What is the maximum value?
quiz.explain: Corners give Z = 0, 120, 110, 50. The largest is 120 at (30, 0).
quiz.mistake: Assumes the intersection corner (20, 30) must be optimal

quiz.q: Minimise Z = 200x + 500y subject to x + 2y ≥ 10, 3x + 4y ≤ 24, x, y ≥ 0. The corners are (0, 5), (4, 3), (0, 6). What is the minimum value?
quiz.mistake: Picks the corner on an axis without evaluating

quiz.q: The furniture dealer maximises Z = 250x + 75y over corners (0, 0), (20, 0), (10, 50), (0, 60). What is the maximum profit?
quiz.explain: Z values: 0, 5000, 6250, 4500. Maximum ₹6250 by buying 10 tables and 50 chairs.
quiz.mistake: Picks the corner with the most tables

quiz.q: According to Theorem 2, a bounded feasible region guarantees
options: both a maximum and a minimum of Z at corner points
quiz.explain: A linear function on a bounded (closed) region attains both extremes, at corners.
steps: Theorem 2: bounded feasible region ⇒ Z has both a maximum and a minimum
Answer: both a maximum and a minimum of Z at corner points
quiz.mistake: Thinks bounded regions can fail to have an optimum

quiz.q: Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + 2y ≤ 10, 3x + y ≤ 15, x, y ≥ 0. Corners are (0, 0), (5, 0), (4, 3), (0, 5). What is the maximum?
steps: Bounded region, so the largest value is the maximum
quiz.mistake: Stops at the first large value

quiz.q: For the same problem, how was the corner (4, 3) found?
options: By solving x + 2y = 10 and 3x + y = 15 together
quiz.explain: From 3x + y = 15, y = 15 − 3x; then x + 30 − 6x = 10 gives x = 4, y = 3.
steps: (4, 3) is where the boundary lines x + 2y = 10 and 3x + y = 15 meet
Answer: By solving x + 2y = 10 and 3x + y = 15 together
quiz.mistake: Guesses the corner instead of solving the boundary equations

quiz.q: Why do we need to check only the corner points?
options: Because the optimal value of a linear objective occurs at a corner point
Because corners are easy to compute
Because Z is zero inside the region
quiz.explain: This is Theorem 1 of linear programming.
steps: Theorem 1: an optimal value of a linear Z occurs at a corner point
So comparing Z at the corners is enough
Answer: Because the optimal value of a linear objective occurs at a corner point
quiz.mistake: Thinks interior points are not allowed

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In a bounded feasible region, the minimum of Z = x + y is at a corner point.
Reason (R): A linear function on a bounded feasible region attains its extreme values at corner points.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: R is the corner point theorem, which directly gives A.
steps: R: on a bounded region a linear Z attains its max and min at corners — true
Z = x + y is linear, so its minimum is at a corner: A follows from R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks minima occur inside the region

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'There are infinitely many feasible points. How do I find the best one?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Check only the corner points, compute Z at each, and pick the best. Corners rule!
teach.nudge: Which special points of the region do you test?

revise.summary: If an LPP has an optimal value, it occurs at a corner point; on a bounded region Z has both a maximum and a minimum there. Evaluate Z at every corner and pick the best.
focus: Make a table of Z at each corner
Find the maximum or minimum and where it occurs
Know Theorems 1 and 2
remember: Theorem 1: optimum (if any) is at a corner
Theorem 2: bounded region ⇒ both max and min exist at corners
State the answer as value and point
traps: Don't assume the intersection corner is always optimal
Evaluate Z at every corner
Compute each Z value carefully

topics.title: Unbounded regions, multiple optima and no solution

learn.hook: Sometimes the feasible region runs off to infinity, sometimes two corners tie, and sometimes no point works at all. Each case needs a careful extra check.
points: Unbounded region, minimum candidate m at a corner: m is the minimum only if the open half-plane Z < m has no point in common with the region. For a maximum M, check Z > M.
If that half-plane does meet the region, the optimum does not exist (e.g. no maximum).
Multiple optimal solutions: if two adjacent corners give the same optimal value, every point on the segment joining them is optimal.
No feasible region: if the constraints have no common point, the LPP has no solution.
Word problems (diet, manufacturing, allocation) often give unbounded regions with ≥ constraints; check them carefully.

example.q: Minimise Z = x + 2y subject to 2x + y ≥ 3, x + 2y ≥ 6, x, y ≥ 0.
steps: The region is unbounded with corners (6, 0) and (0, 3).
x + 2y < 6 has no common point with the region (it contradicts x + 2y ≥ 6).
So the minimum 6 is attained at every point of the segment joining (6, 0) and (0, 3).
example.answer: Minimum Z = 6 at all points on the segment from (6, 0) to (0, 3)

learn.reallife: Planning a school meal that meets minimum calorie and protein norms (like those set under the PM POSHAN mid-day meal scheme) at the lowest cost is a diet LPP; its ≥ constraints usually give an unbounded feasible region.

games.title: Which case?
items: Two adjacent corners give the same best Z
Bounded region, one corner gives the largest Z
Max 4x + y with x + y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 90

games.title: Special cases
items: An unbounded region never has a minimum.
It may, if the half-plane Z < m misses the region.
If Z > M meets an unbounded region, Z has no maximum there.
Z can be made larger than M.
Two corners with the same optimal Z give infinitely many optimal points.
Every point on the segment between them is optimal.
x − y ≤ −1 and −x + y ≤ 0 (with x, y ≥ 0) have a common region.
The first needs y ≥ x + 1 and the second y ≤ x.
A bounded feasible region always has both a maximum and a minimum.

quiz.q: Minimise Z = 3x + 5y subject to x + 3y ≥ 3, x + y ≥ 2, x, y ≥ 0. The corners are (3, 0), (3/2, 1/2), (0, 2). What is the minimum?
quiz.explain: Z: 9, 4.5 + 2.5 = 7, 10. The smallest is 7, and 3x + 5y < 7 has no point in common with the region, so the minimum is 7 at (3/2, 1/2).
quiz.mistake: Takes the smallest corner value without checking the unbounded region, or slips in arithmetic

quiz.q: Maximise Z = −x + 2y subject to x ≥ 3, x + y ≥ 5, x + 2y ≥ 6, y ≥ 0. The corners give Z = −6, −2, 1. What is the conclusion?
options: Z has no maximum, since −x + 2y > 1 meets the region
quiz.explain: The region is unbounded upward; e.g. (3, 10) is feasible with Z = 17 > 1. So no maximum exists.
steps: Largest corner value is 1, but the region is unbounded, so check −x + 2y > 1
So Z > 1 meets the region and Z can grow without limit
Answer: Z has no maximum, since −x + 2y > 1 meets the region
quiz.mistake: Accepts the largest corner value without the half-plane check

quiz.q: Maximise Z = x + y subject to x − y ≤ −1, −x + y ≤ 0, x, y ≥ 0. What happens?
options: There is no feasible region, so no maximum
The region is unbounded with no maximum
quiz.explain: x − y ≤ −1 gives y ≥ x + 1, while −x + y ≤ 0 gives y ≤ x. These cannot both hold.
steps: y cannot be both ≥ x + 1 and ≤ x: no common point
Answer: There is no feasible region, so no maximum
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the constraints contradict each other

quiz.q: Minimise Z = x + 2y with 2x + y ≥ 3, x + 2y ≥ 6, x, y ≥ 0. How many points give the minimum value?
quiz.explain: Z(6, 0) = Z(0, 3) = 6, and every point of the segment between them gives Z = 6.
steps: Z(6, 0) = 6 and Z(0, 3) = 6: two adjacent corners give the same minimum
x + 2y < 6 has no common point with the region
So every point on the segment joining them gives Z = 6
quiz.mistake: Counts only the two corners

quiz.q: A diet uses x kg of food P (₹4/kg) and y kg of food Q (₹6/kg) with 2x + y ≥ 8 and x + 2y ≥ 10. The corners are (10, 0), (2, 4), (0, 8). What is the minimum cost?
quiz.explain: Z = 4x + 6y: 40, 8 + 24 = 32, 48. Since 4x + 6y < 32 has no common point with the region, ₹32 at (2, 4) is the minimum.
steps: Unbounded region: 4x + 6y < 32 has no common point with it, so 32 is the minimum
quiz.mistake: Picks a corner on an axis

quiz.q: In the diet problem, how is the corner (2, 4) obtained?
steps: Answer: By solving 2x + y = 8 and x + 2y = 10
quiz.mistake: Guesses instead of solving

quiz.q: For an unbounded region with smallest corner value m, when is m the minimum of Z?
options: When the half-plane Z < m has no point in common with the feasible region
quiz.explain: If some feasible point had Z < m, then m would not be the minimum.
steps: On an unbounded region, a smaller Z might occur far away from the corners
m is the minimum only if no feasible point has Z < m
Answer: When the half-plane Z < m has no point in common with the feasible region
quiz.mistake: Assumes the corner rule works without checking for unbounded regions

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If the feasible region is unbounded, a maximum of Z may not exist.
Reason (R): On an unbounded region, Z can sometimes be made arbitrarily large.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: When Z grows without bound along the region, there is no maximum, which is what A says.
steps: R: on an unbounded region Z may increase without limit — true
If Z is unbounded above, no maximum exists: that is A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks every LPP has a maximum

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What do I do if the feasible region goes on forever?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Draw Z < m (or Z > M). If it misses the region, the corner value is optimal; if it meets it, there is no optimum!
teach.nudge: What extra check do unbounded regions need?

revise.summary: On an unbounded region, the best corner value is the optimum only if the open half-plane beyond it misses the region. Equal values at two adjacent corners give infinitely many optimal points, and contradictory constraints give no solution.
focus: Do the half-plane check for unbounded regions
Recognise multiple optimal solutions
Recognise an empty feasible region
remember: Min m is valid if Z < m has no common point with the region
Max M is valid if Z > M has no common point with the region
Two adjacent optimal corners ⇒ every point on the segment is optimal
traps: Don't accept the largest corner value on an unbounded region without checking
Two corners with the same optimum mean infinitely many solutions, not two
Check that the constraints can all hold together

learn.hook: The chance of rain today is 30%. But if dark clouds are already rolling in over Mumbai, that chance jumps. New information changes probability: that is conditional probability.
points: Recall: for equally likely outcomes, P(E) = n(E)/n(S); in general 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1 and P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F) − P(E ∩ F).
Conditional probability of E given F: P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F), provided P(F) ≠ 0.
For equally likely outcomes, P(E|F) = n(E ∩ F)/n(F): F becomes the new, reduced sample space.
P(E|F) and P(F|E) are generally different.
Read 'given that', 'if it is known that' as the condition F.

example.q: A fair die is thrown. Find the probability that it shows 4, given that the number is even.
steps: F = even = {2, 4, 6}, so the reduced sample space has 3 outcomes.

learn.reallife: Doctors read test results using conditional probability: the chance of a disease given a positive result is very different from the chance of a positive result given the disease.

items.q: Two coins: P(both heads | first is head)

games.title: Find P(E|F) by reducing the sample space
items: List the outcomes in E ∩ F

quiz.q: P(E) = 0.6, P(F) = 0.3 and P(E ∩ F) = 0.2. What is P(E|F)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by P(E) instead of P(F)

quiz.q: For the same data, what is P(F|E)?
quiz.explain: P(F|E) = 0.2/0.6 = 1/3, which differs from P(E|F).
quiz.mistake: Assumes P(F|E) = P(E|F)

quiz.q: A family has two children. Given that at least one is a boy, what is the probability that both are boys?
quiz.explain: Given set: {BB, BG, GB}. Only BB works: 1/3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that BG and GB are different outcomes

quiz.q: A family has two children. Given that the elder is a boy, what is the probability that both are boys?
quiz.explain: Given set: {BB, BG}. Only BB: 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Treats it like the 'at least one boy' problem

quiz.q: A coin is tossed three times. Find P(at least two heads | first toss is a head).
quiz.explain: F = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT}. E ∩ F = {HHH, HHT, HTH}. P = 3/4.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full sample space of 8 outcomes

quiz.q: Two dice are thrown. Given that the first die shows 5, what is the probability that the sum is at least 10?
quiz.explain: Second die must be 5 or 6: 2 out of 6.
quiz.mistake: Counts outcomes in the full 36-outcome space

quiz.q: Why must P(F) ≠ 0 in P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F)?
options: We cannot condition on an impossible event, and we cannot divide by zero
Because E and F are independent
quiz.explain: If F cannot happen, 'given F' makes no sense, and the formula would divide by zero.
steps: P(E|F) is the chance of E when F is known to have happened
If P(F) = 0, F cannot happen, so 'given F' has no meaning
Also the formula P(E ∩ F)/P(F) would divide by 0
Answer: We cannot condition on an impossible event, and we cannot divide by zero
quiz.mistake: Thinks the condition is on P(E)

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For a die, P(number is 2 | number is even) = 1/3.
Reason (R): Given F, the sample space reduces to the outcomes of F.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Reduced space {2, 4, 6} has 3 outcomes, one of which is 2. R explains A.
steps: R: given F, the sample space reduces to F — true
F = even = {2, 4, 6}, 3 outcomes; E ∩ F = {2}, 1 outcome
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Uses 1/6 from the full sample space

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does P(E|F) mean, and how do I calculate it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! P(E|F) is the chance of E once F is known: P(E ∩ F)/P(F), like shrinking the sample space to F!
teach.nudge: What do you divide by, and why?

revise.summary: P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F) is the probability of E when F is known to have happened, with P(F) ≠ 0. For equally likely outcomes, F becomes the new sample space.
focus: Compute P(E|F) from given probabilities
Use the reduced sample space for dice, coins and families
Tell P(E|F) from P(F|E)
traps: Divide by P(F), the given event, not by P(E)
'At least one boy' and 'elder is a boy' give different reduced spaces
Don't use the full sample space after conditioning

learn.hook: Conditional probability is a full probability in its own right: it obeys the same rules, just inside the smaller world F.
points: P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) − P((A ∩ B)|F); if A and B are disjoint, the last term is 0.
Typical settings: dice, coins, cards and families with children.
With cards, remember: 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 4 aces/kings/queens/jacks, 26 red and 26 black, 12 face cards.

example.q: A card is drawn from a pack of 52. Given that it is red, find the probability that it is a king.

learn.reallife: Cricket statisticians quote 'probability of winning given the team bats first'. Its complement, the probability of not winning given batting first, is 1 minus that value.

games.title: Property check
items: Given F has happened, F is certain.
Complements work inside the reduced space.
The complement rule is P(E|F) + P(E′|F) = 1, not this.
If A and B are disjoint, P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F).

quiz.q: If P(E|F) = 0.4, what is P(E′|F)?
quiz.mistake: Thinks the complement rule does not apply to conditional probability

quiz.q: P(A|F) = 0.5, P(B|F) = 0.3 and P((A ∩ B)|F) = 0.1. What is P((A ∪ B)|F)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the intersection

quiz.q: A card is drawn from a pack of 52. Given that it is a face card, what is the probability that it is a queen?
quiz.explain: There are 12 face cards, 4 of them queens: 4/12 = 1/3.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full pack of 52

quiz.q: Two dice are thrown. Given that a doublet appears, what is the probability that the sum is 6?
quiz.explain: Doublets: 6 outcomes. Sum 6 among them: (3, 3) only. 1/6.
quiz.mistake: Counts all ways to get sum 6 (5 ways)

quiz.q: What is P(S|F) for any event F with P(F) ≠ 0?
steps: S ∩ F = F, so P(S|F) = P(F)/P(F)
quiz.mistake: Confuses P(S|F) with P(F)

quiz.q: A die is rolled. E = {1, 3, 5}, F = {1, 2, 3}. What is P(E′|F)?
quiz.mistake: Gives P(E|F) instead of its complement

quiz.q: A coin is tossed twice. Given that at least one tail appears, what is the probability of exactly one head?
quiz.explain: Given set {HT, TH, TT}; exactly one head: HT, TH. 2/3.
quiz.mistake: Uses the 4-outcome sample space

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): P(E|F) + P(E′|F) = 1.
Reason (R): E and E′ are disjoint and together make up the whole sample space.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: Using the union rule for disjoint events, P((E ∪ E′)|F) = P(S|F) = 1, which gives A.
steps: R: E ∩ E′ = φ and E ∪ E′ = S — true
So P(E|F) + P(E′|F) = P((E ∪ E′)|F) = P(S|F) = 1
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks complements need independence

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Do the usual probability rules still work for conditional probability?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Yes! Complements, unions and P(F|F) = 1 all work inside the reduced space F. Same rules, smaller world!
teach.nudge: What is P(E′|F) in terms of P(E|F)?

revise.summary: Conditional probability follows the usual rules within F: P(S|F) = 1, the union rule, and P(E′|F) = 1 − P(E|F).
focus: Use the complement and union rules for conditional probability
Solve card, dice and coin problems with a condition
remember: P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) − P((A ∩ B)|F)
Pack: 52 cards, 13 per suit, 12 face cards, 26 red
traps: Subtract the intersection in the union rule
Use 12 face cards, not 52, when the card is known to be a face card
Don't give P(E|F) when its complement is asked

learn.hook: Draw two cards one after the other without putting the first back. The second draw depends on the first, and the multiplication theorem handles that chain.
points: P(E ∩ F) = P(E) P(F|E) = P(F) P(E|F), for P(E), P(F) ≠ 0.
For three events: P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E) P(F|E) P(G|E ∩ F).
Without replacement, the counts change after each draw: numerator and denominator both drop.
Read problems in order: first draw, then second given the first, and so on.
Sanity check: the answer can never be larger than any single probability in the chain.

quiz.mistake: Keeps the denominator 10 for every draw, getting 3/100

quiz.q: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(first red, second blue)?
quiz.mistake: Keeps 8 in the second denominator

quiz.q: P(E) = 0.5 and P(F|E) = 0.4. What is P(E ∩ F)?
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of multiplying

quiz.q: A box has 4 defective and 16 good bulbs. Two are taken without replacement. What is P(both defective)?
quiz.mistake: Uses 4/20 for both draws

quiz.q: Which formula gives P(E ∩ F ∩ G)?
quiz.explain: The multiplication theorem extends step by step, each factor conditioned on everything before it.
steps: Multiplication theorem, one event at a time
P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E) × P(F|E) × P(G|E ∩ F)
Each factor is conditioned on everything before it; P(E)P(F)P(G) needs independence
quiz.mistake: Assumes independence without being told

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): When drawing two balls without replacement, P(second red | first red) is less than P(first red) if the bag has both colours.
Reason (R): After removing a red ball, the proportion of red balls in the bag decreases.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With r red out of n (r < n), (r − 1)/(n − 1) < r/n. R explains why.
steps: With r red in n balls (0 < r < n): P(first red) = r/n
P(second red | first red) = (r − 1)/(n − 1), and (r − 1)/(n − 1) < r/n since r < n
R: removing a red ball lowers the red proportion — that is the reason
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the second probability stays the same

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the chance that two things happen one after another?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Multiply P(first) by P(second given first), updating the counts if nothing is replaced!
teach.nudge: What changes in the second fraction when you do not replace?

revise.summary: P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F|E), and for three events P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F|E)P(G|E ∩ F). Without replacement, the counts change after each draw.
focus: Find probabilities of successive draws without replacement
Use P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F|E)
Extend to three events
remember: Without replacement: reduce both numerator and denominator
traps: Don't keep the same denominator on later draws
Multiply, don't add, for 'and'
Don't assume independence unless told

learn.hook: Tossing a coin in Delhi does not change a die roll in Chennai. Such events are independent: knowing one tells you nothing about the other.
points: E and F are independent if P(E|F) = P(E) (with P(F) ≠ 0), equivalently P(E ∩ F) = P(E) P(F).
Independent is NOT the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive means P(E ∩ F) = 0.
Two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.
E, F, G are mutually independent if P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), P(F ∩ G) = P(F)P(G), P(E ∩ G) = P(E)P(G) and P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F)P(G).
Pairwise independence alone does not guarantee mutual independence.

example.q: A die is thrown. E = multiple of 3, F = even number. Are E and F independent?
example.answer: Yes, E and F are independent.

learn.reallife: Safety systems often use independent backups: if each fails rarely and independently, the chance of all failing together is the product of the small chances, which is tiny.

games.title: Independent or mutually exclusive?
items: First toss head; second toss head
Card is a king; same card is a queen
Student passes; same student fails the same exam

games.title: Independence facts
items: If P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), A and B are independent.
Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are independent.
Pairwise independence of three events implies mutual independence.
The triple product condition is also needed.
Successive tosses of a fair coin are independent.
One toss does not affect another.
The bag is restored each time.

quiz.q: A and B are independent with P(A) = 1/2 and P(B) = 1/3. What is P(A ∩ B)?
quiz.explain: Independence gives P(A ∩ B) = (1/2)(1/3) = 1/6.
quiz.mistake: Adds the probabilities

quiz.q: With the same independent A and B (P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3), what is P(A ∪ B)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract P(A ∩ B)

quiz.q: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4 and A, B are independent. What is P(A ∪ B)?
quiz.mistake: Treats A and B as mutually exclusive

quiz.q: A die is thrown. E = {1, 3, 5} (odd) and F = {1, 2, 3}. Are E and F independent?
options: No, since P(E ∩ F) = 1/3 but P(E)P(F) = 1/4
No, since they are mutually exclusive
quiz.explain: E ∩ F = {1, 3}, probability 1/3, which is not (1/2)(1/2).
steps: Answer: No, since P(E ∩ F) = 1/3 but P(E)P(F) = 1/4
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal probabilities mean independence

quiz.q: Which statement is true for events A and B with P(A), P(B) > 0?
options: If they are mutually exclusive, they are not independent
If they are independent, they are mutually exclusive
Mutually exclusive events always have P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
quiz.explain: Mutually exclusive gives P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B).
steps: Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) > 0 when both are positive
Both cannot hold, so mutually exclusive events are not independent
Answer: If they are mutually exclusive, they are not independent
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'independent' with 'cannot happen together'

quiz.q: A card is drawn from 52. E = 'spade', F = 'ace'. What is P(E ∩ F)?
quiz.explain: Only the ace of spades: 1/52, which equals (1/4)(1/13), so E and F are independent.
quiz.mistake: Adds P(E) and P(F)

quiz.q: For mutual independence of E, F and G, which extra condition is needed besides pairwise independence?
options: E, F, G are mutually exclusive
quiz.explain: Mutual independence needs all three pairwise products and the triple product.
steps: Pairwise: P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), P(F ∩ G) = P(F)P(G), P(E ∩ G) = P(E)P(G)
Mutual independence also needs the triple product rule
quiz.mistake: Thinks pairwise independence is enough

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If A and B are independent, then P(A|B) = P(A).
Reason (R): P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = P(A)P(B)/P(B).
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Substituting the independence condition in the definition gives P(A|B) = P(A).
steps: R: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = P(A)P(B)/P(B) = P(A) — true
So A follows directly from R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the two definitions of independence

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Independent and mutually exclusive sound the same. Are they?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Independent means one doesn't change the other's chance, so P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Mutually exclusive means they can't happen together!
teach.nudge: What is P(A ∩ B) for independent events, and for mutually exclusive ones?

revise.summary: E and F are independent when P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), i.e. knowing F does not change P(E). Independent events are not the same as mutually exclusive events.
focus: Test independence by comparing P(E ∩ F) and P(E)P(F)
Use independence to find P(A ∩ B) and P(A ∪ B)
Know the conditions for three events
remember: Independent ⇔ P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F) ⇔ P(E|F) = P(E)
Mutual independence of three needs pairwise and triple product rules
traps: Independent does not mean mutually exclusive
Equal probabilities do not prove independence
Pairwise independence is not enough for mutual independence

learn.hook: Three bowlers each have a small chance of taking a wicket this over. What is the chance at least one of them does? Flip the question: find the chance none does.
points: If E and F are independent, so are E and F′, E′ and F, and E′ and F′.
P(E′ ∩ F′) = P(E′)P(F′) = (1 − P(E))(1 − P(F)) for independent E, F.
P(at least one of E, F, G) = 1 − P(none) = 1 − P(E′)P(F′)P(G′) for independent events.
With replacement, successive draws are independent; multiply the same probabilities.
To test independence, compare P(E ∩ F) with P(E)P(F).

quiz.q: A coin is tossed 3 times. What is P(at least one head)?
quiz.explain: P(no head) = (1/2)³ = 1/8, so P(at least one) = 7/8.
quiz.mistake: Counts only exactly one head

quiz.q: A solves a problem with probability 1/2 and B with 1/3, independently. What is P(the problem is solved)?
quiz.explain: P(neither) = (1/2)(2/3) = 1/3, so P(solved) = 2/3.

quiz.q: P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4, independent. What is P(A ∩ B′)?
quiz.explain: A and B′ are independent: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18.
quiz.mistake: Uses P(B) instead of P(B′)

quiz.q: Two cards are drawn with replacement from 52. What is P(both kings)?
quiz.explain: With replacement the draws are independent: (1/13)(1/13) = 1/169.
quiz.mistake: Uses the without-replacement answer

quiz.q: A die is thrown twice. What is P(at least one six)?
quiz.explain: P(no six) = (5/6)² = 25/36, so the answer is 11/36.
quiz.mistake: Adds 1/6 + 1/6 and double-counts (6, 6)

quiz.q: If E and F are independent with P(E) = 0.2 and P(F) = 0.5, what is P(E′ ∩ F′)?
steps: E, F independent ⇒ E′, F′ independent
quiz.mistake: Computes 1 − P(E)P(F)

quiz.q: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3 and P(A′ ∪ B′) = 5/6. Are A and B independent?
quiz.explain: By De Morgan, A′ ∪ B′ = (A ∩ B)′, so P(A ∩ B) = 1 − 5/6 = 1/6, which equals (1/2)(1/3).
steps: Answer: Yes, since P(A ∩ B) = 1/6 = P(A)P(B)
quiz.mistake: Forgets De Morgan's law A′ ∪ B′ = (A ∩ B)′

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If A and B are independent, then A′ and B′ are independent.
Reason (R): P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B) = (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)) when A, B are independent.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 1 − P(A) − P(B) + P(A)P(B) factorises as P(A′)P(B′), which is exactly the independence of A′ and B′.
steps: This factorises as (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)) = P(A′)P(B′) — so R is true
P(A′ ∩ B′) = P(A′)P(B′) is exactly independence of A′ and B′
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks complements of independent events are dependent

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the fastest way to find the chance that at least one thing happens?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Find P(none) by multiplying the complements, then 1 minus that. At least one, at lightning speed!
teach.nudge: Instead of adding cases, which single event do you subtract from 1?

revise.summary: If E and F are independent, so are their complements. 'At least one' is easiest as 1 − P(none), multiplying the complement probabilities for independent events.
focus: Use 1 − P(none) for 'at least one'
Find P(A ∩ B′) and P(A′ ∩ B′) for independent events
Use De Morgan to test independence
traps: Don't add probabilities for 'at least one'
P(E′ ∩ F′) is not 1 − P(E)P(F)
Use P(B′), not P(B), in P(A ∩ B′)

learn.hook: A red ball comes out, but which bag did it come from? Bayes' theorem runs probability backwards: from the result to the cause.
points: E₁, E₂, …, Eₙ form a partition of S if they are pairwise disjoint, together make up S, and each has non-zero probability.
Theorem of total probability: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ) P(A|Eᵢ).
Bayes' theorem: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ) P(A|Eᵢ) / Σⱼ P(Eⱼ) P(A|Eⱼ).
Proof idea: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ ∩ A)/P(A); write the top with the multiplication theorem and the bottom with total probability.
The Eᵢ are hypotheses; P(Eᵢ) are prior probabilities and P(Eᵢ|A) are posterior probabilities (after A is observed).

example.q: Bag I has 3 red and 4 black balls; bag II has 5 red and 6 black. A bag is chosen at random and a ball drawn is red. Find P(it came from bag II).

learn.reallife: Many email spam filters use Bayes' theorem: given that certain words appear, what is the chance that the message is spam?

games.title: Applying Bayes' theorem

Divide the required P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) by P(A)

quiz.q: Bag I has 3 red, 4 black; bag II has 5 red, 6 black. A bag is chosen at random and a red ball is drawn. What is P(bag II | red)?

quiz.q: Bag A has 2 red and 3 white balls; bag B has 4 red and 1 white. A bag is chosen at random and one ball is drawn. What is P(red)?
quiz.mistake: Adds the bag probabilities without the 1/2 weights

quiz.q: For the same bags, given the ball is red, what is P(it came from bag A)?

quiz.q: Which conditions make E₁, E₂, E₃ a partition of S?

steps: Partition: no two of E₁, E₂, E₃ overlap
Together they make up S, and each has non-zero probability
They need not be equally likely or independent
Answer: Pairwise disjoint, union is S, each with non-zero probability
quiz.mistake: Thinks the parts must be equally likely

quiz.q: In Bayes' theorem, the probability P(Eᵢ|A) is called the
quiz.explain: It is the updated probability after A is observed.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up prior and posterior

quiz.q: Bayes' theorem is derived by combining the definition of conditional probability with
options: the multiplication theorem and the theorem of total probability

steps: Answer: the multiplication theorem and the theorem of total probability
quiz.mistake: Assumes independence is needed

quiz.q: Two bags are equally likely. Bag I: P(red) = 1/4; bag II: P(red) = 3/4. A red ball is drawn. What is P(bag II | red)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by P(red)

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In the theorem of total probability, the events Eᵢ must form a partition of S.
Reason (R): Then A is the disjoint union of the events A ∩ Eᵢ.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because A = ∪(A ∩ Eᵢ) with disjoint pieces, P(A) = Σ P(A ∩ Eᵢ) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ). R is the reason.
steps: R: if the Eᵢ form a partition, A = (A ∩ E₁) ∪ (A ∩ E₂) ∪ …, with disjoint pieces — true
So P(A) = Σ P(A ∩ Eᵢ) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ)
That is why a partition is required: R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Uses overlapping events, which double-counts

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does Bayes' theorem do, and how do I use it?'

revise.summary: If E₁, …, Eₙ partition S, then P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) (total probability). Bayes' theorem reverses the condition: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ)/Σ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ).
focus: Find P(A) by total probability
Find a posterior probability with Bayes' theorem
Know the meaning of partition, prior and posterior
remember: Partition: disjoint, union S, each P(Eᵢ) > 0

Weight each bag or group by its prior
Don't report the prior as the answer

learn.hook: A test is 99% accurate, yet a positive result may still mean only about a 1-in-6 chance of disease. Bayes' theorem explains this surprise.

quiz.mistake: Uses only his truth rate 3/4

quiz.q: 0.1% of people have a disease. A test detects it 99% of the time and gives a false positive 0.5% of the time. What is P(disease | positive)?
quiz.mistake: Assumes the posterior equals the test's accuracy

quiz.q: An insurer has 2000 scooter, 4000 car and 6000 truck drivers with accident probabilities 0.01, 0.03 and 0.15. An insured person has an accident. What is P(scooter driver)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the scooter share 1/6 as the answer

quiz.q: For the same insurer, what is P(truck driver | accident)?
quiz.explain: Using the scaled weights 0.01, 0.06, 0.45: 0.45/0.52 = 45/52.
quiz.mistake: Uses the truck share 1/2

quiz.q: In a class, 40% are girls and 60% are boys. 25% of girls and 10% of boys got an A grade. A student with an A is picked. What is P(the student is a girl)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the prior 40% as the answer

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Even a 99% accurate test can give a low P(disease | positive) for a rare disease.
Reason (R): When the prior is very small, false positives from the large healthy group can outnumber true positives.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: In the 0.1% example, true positives are 0.00099 while false positives are 0.004995, about five times more. That gives a posterior near 0.165.
steps: False positives are about 5 times the true positives, so P(disease | positive) ≈ 0.165
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Ignores the prior probability

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: 'A test is 99% accurate and I tested positive. Am I 99% likely to be sick?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Not necessarily! If the disease is rare, false positives from healthy people pile up, and Bayes' theorem gives a much lower chance!
teach.nudge: What role does how rare the disease is play?

revise.summary: Bayes' theorem answers 'which source caused it' questions for factories, tests, truth-tellers and insurance groups. Weight each source by its share, then divide by the total probability.
focus: Set up priors and likelihoods from a word problem
Compute the posterior for one source
Explain why rare-disease tests can mislead
remember: Rare events: false positives from the large group can outnumber true positives
traps: Don't use a machine's output share as the answer
Don't assume P(disease | positive) equals test accuracy
Scale percentages consistently before dividing
